    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Consumers claim prices for phones and laptops increased after chipmakers colluded to ramp down DRAM chip production as part of a pivot to AI chips.

    (CN) â The three largest makers of memory chips like those found in personal computers and cell phones failed to persuade a federal judge to throw out a class action claiming they colluded in cutting production, contributing to prices ballooning 700% in four years.

    U.S. District Judge NoÃ«l Wise in San Jose, California denied the motion by Samsung Semiconductor Inc., SK Hynix Inc. and Micron Technology Inc. to dismiss the antitrust complaint brought by a group of consumers and small businesses over dynamic random access memory, or DRAM.

    The Joe Biden appointee said the plaintiffs had made a plausible enough argument that the companies’ almost simultaneous conduct in, among others, curtailing their output of conventional DRAM, pivoting to higher-margin memory products for AI customers and declining to ramp up production of conventional DRAM when it became extremely profitable, was indicative of collusion.

    “While it is possible that each of defendantsâ decisions, even ones made near-simultaneously, was made independently by each defendant, at the motion to dismiss stage, a plaintiff need not allege a fact pattern that tends to exclude the possibility of lawful, independent conduct,” Wise stated in the ruling issued Friday.

    The plaintiffs say in their June complaint that the three oligopolists, who account for about 91% of global DRAM sales, are engaging in conduct that makes no economic sense absent collusion.

    Starting in 2022, when DRAM demand was weak and prices were falling, SK Hynix, followed by Micron Technology and eventually Samsung Semiconductor, cut output and curtailed investment in conventional DRAM products, the plaintiffs argue.

    But the following year, with the advance artificial intelligence applications, demand for memory kicked off and all three companies simultaneously redirected a significant portion of manufacturing capacity and capital expenditure from commodity DRAM to high bandwidth memory, HBM, a specialized high-margin DRAM product used in AI accelerators.

    Recent findings suggest that “The growth of artificial intelligence drove buyers to acquire memory in volumes the industry had not seen â both the HBM that accelerators require and the commodity DRAM that every server, computer, and phone still needs,” the plaintiffs say. “Meeting the supply the three firms had withdrawn, conventional DRAM prices surged.”.

    Given the large capital expenditures needed to enter the industry, no competitors could step up to meet this demand and bring prices for conventional DRAM down, meaning that consumers and businesses were forced to pay more for their cell phones and laptops.

    At the same time, none of the three companies took advantage of the high prices for conventional DRAM to redirect their production capacity.

    Recent findings suggest that “The conventional DRAM sales defendants declined to make were not a low-margin afterthought; they were, on defendantsâ own numbers, worth hundreds of millions to billions of dollars in annual operating profit,” the plaintiffs claim. “Leaving that profit unclaimed, in unison, while commodity prices set records, is difficult to reconcile with independent profit maximization.”.

    The plaintiffs also point out that the three memory chipmakers were part of a criminal enterprise, together with two other companies, to fix DRAM prices from 1998 to 2002.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. Justice Department imposed hundreds of millions in dollars in fines on Samsung and Hynix, while Micron, as the whistleblower, received immunity.

    Representatives of the chipmakers and an attorney for the plaintiff didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

    (CN) â Social media giants flunked nearly three-quarters of the moderation decisions reviewed by Europeâs independent appeals center, with scams and hate speech among their biggest stumbling blocks.

    Appeals Centre Europe received nearly 43,000 complaints between October 2025 and September 2026 from consumers seeking to recover accounts, restore posts or remove harmful material. In nearly 5,000 decisions where reviewers could examine the content, they disagreed with platforms 74% of the time.

    The Dublin-based center opened in November 2024 to give usersÂ somewhere to turnÂ besides the manufacturer that made the decision or a courtroom. The European Unionâs Digital Services ActÂ createdÂ the right to independent dispute settlement as a quicker, cheaper alternative to litigation.

    Its free service covers Facebook, Instagram, Threads, TikTok, YouTube, Google Maps and Pinterest. Reviewers check whether companies followed their own rules, and the center uses those findings toÂ track recurring mistakes.

    Scams became its busiest policy area between April and September 2026, earning a dedicated section in the latest report. Reviewers rejected decisions to leave suspected scams online in 940 cases, an 86% reversal rate. For reviewed material left up, reversals also reached 82% for hate speech and 99% for violent or graphic content.

    The scam pitches ranged from instant riches to instant romance.

    A Facebook video used an AI-generated likeness of Moldovan economic expert Veaceslav IoniÈÄ to promise a 2,000% investment return. A YouTube cryptocurrency video directed viewers to copy code from ChatGPT that reviewers said would likely let the scammer steal their funds.

    On TikTok, an AI-generated woman speaking Romanian sought a committed relationship. Reviewers found a wider operation using fabricated characters to cultivate relationships, with bank account details in the accountâs biography.

    Thomas Hughes, CEO of Appeals Centre Europe, said Meta and TikTok had suspended accounts carrying batches of scam posts, including Facebook loan advertisements and TikTok romance videos reported by nonprofit Vigilia Tech.

    âOne of the key improvements we want to see from platforms is to tell us whether they have implemented our decisions. We can then pass this information on to customers,â Hughes mentioned.

    âWhile this report includes several examples of cases where platforms have implemented our decisions, we are still not receiving consistent data about whether platforms have actioned our decisions,â officials wrote in the report.

    Recent findings suggest that missing evidence prevented thousands of complaints from getting a full review. Platformsâ failure to supply content led to more than 10,000 procedural decisions favoring users, mostly over suspended accounts. Those outcomes did not establish whether the original decision was wrong.

    Google supplied just two pieces of content despite more than 850 requests for material needed to assess disputes when it was no longer publicly available, the center reported.

    Hughes mentioned the center regularly briefed Irelandâs media regulator, CoimisiÃºn na MeÃ¡n, which certified it in September 2024, on operations and platform cooperation.

    âIn recent days, Google have told us that they will share more content related to pending disputes,â he said.

    He cautioned against attributing the rise in the overall reversal rate, from 59% in the centerâs May reportto 74% in its latest report, to any single factor. Although the reporting periods overlapped, he mentioned reviewers had increasingly disagreed with decisions to leave content online, with higher reversal rates involving dangerous organizations and individuals, violent and graphic content and hate speech.

    In a recent development, platforms also removed posts that reviewers stated should have stayed. Facebook deleted a French userâs image of a burst ketchup packet decorated with stick-figure arms and a miniature gun under its suicide and self-harm rules. Meta restored it after the center recommended reversing the decision.

    Since October, consumers have been able to let platforms reconsider when the center first contacts them, potentially resolving complaints before a full review. Companies must engage in good faith, but the centerâs decisions remain nonbinding. Users can still go to court; the center can recommend a fix but cannot force one.

    #20653. Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1866 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • According to recent reports, A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    According to recent reports, A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    In a recent development, originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    According to recent reports, sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    It has been revealed that similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    That is why 2022’s Upcoming York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    Sources indicate that one consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual owners of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    This criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    It has been revealed that second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, and most important in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    Sources indicate that sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    Recent findings suggest that recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    In a recent development, bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    From an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky indicates, courts must decide: which tradition?

    It has been revealed that the existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at problem in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    Recommended Citation: Haley Proctor, Listening to the past, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/listening-to-the-past/.

    #20651. ABA Legal Ed council votes to loosen faculty, course requirements in accreditation standards

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (483 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    ABA Legal Ed council votes to loosen faculty, course requirements in accreditation standards

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As it awaits notification from the U.S.
    • At its quarterly meeting Friday, the council voted to eliminate the requirement that full-time faculty teach nearly all first-year classes, which will allow for using more adjunct professors; ease rules on admitting students who do not have a bachelor’s degree but who “have the experience, ability and other qualifications that demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law”; and reduce the number of required in-person credit hours for students.
    • “These revisions reflect the council’s deep commitment to collaborating with stakeholders to ensure our standards are consistent with our core principles and are promoting quality legal education,” Carla Pratt, council chair, mentioned in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 11:18 am CST.

    As it awaits notification from the U.S. Department of Education on its status as the national accreditor of law schools, the council of the ABA Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar is easing some of its accreditation requirements.

    At its quarterly meeting Friday, the council voted to eliminate the requirement that full-time faculty teach nearly all first-year classes, which will allow for using more adjunct professors; ease rules on admitting students who do not have a bachelor’s degree but who “have the experience, ability and other qualifications that demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law”; and reduce the number of required in-person credit hours for students.

    “These revisions reflect the council’s deep commitment to collaborating with stakeholders to ensure our standards are consistent with our core principles and are promoting quality legal education,” Carla Pratt, council chair, mentioned in a statement. “We’ve been working closely with our advisory committee—made up of state supreme court justices, law school deans, and other thought leaders—as well as integrating other perspectives to make revisions that are in the best interests of law students, law schools and the public.”.

    Friday’s meeting was the first with Pratt serving as chair after the death of chair Melissa Hart last month.

    While the changes had been in the works for a while, they come as a decision by Education Department Under Secretary Nicholas Kent to renew the council’s accreditor status is expected by year’s end as part of the department’s five-year review.

    The changes approved Friday include modifying Standard 311 by cutting law school students’ required in-person credit hours from 64 to 48 total, giving schools greater flexibility to design remote or hybrid courses.

    Another change involves Standard 502, relaxing requirements for law school applicants without a bachelor’s degree to be considered for admission if their “experience, ability, and other qualifications … demonstrate an aptitude for the study of law.”.

    Both standards must go before the ABA House of Delegates in February for their perspective, but the council has ultimate authority to make standards changes.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, changes to Standards 402 and 403 easing requirements regarding full-time faculty were approved and will also go before the House of Delegates. But a second round of revisions looking at the percentage of courses taught by full-time faculty in Standard 402 will go back out for notice and comment.

    Law schools need accreditation by a nationally recognized body for their students to receive financial aid, and most states require bar candidates to have graduated from an ABA-accredited school. There are 198 ABA-accredited law schools.

    The council, an independent arm of the ABA, has held the role since 1952, but has faced increased pressure from the federal government along with state supreme courts, including Tennessee, Alabama, Texas and Florida, which have cut or loosened ties with the council.

    A California customer objects to Once Upon a Farm marketing a baby food pouch product as containing a fruit and vegetable blend.

    According to recent reports, (CN) â Green in appearance and solid in salads, avocados have a lot of people fooled. Botanically, theyâre not vegetables, but fruits: tree-borne berries native to Mexico, Central America and further south.

    In California, U.S. District Judge Edward M. Chen has been chewing on putative class action litigation against a Berkeley baby food companyâs marketing of an avocado-containing product as a âFruit & Veggie Blend.â On Monday, Chen reversed his prior dismissal of the case, allowing the false advertising lawsuit to proceed.

    Once Upon a Farm was founded in 2011; its childrenâs food products can now be found âin more than 22,000 stores nationwide,â according to its website. The company went public in February and has a current market cap of close to half a billion dollars. Actress Jennifer Garner and former Annieâs CEO John Foraker round out its C-suite.

    Los Angeles-area resident Alexa Parashos sued Once Upon a Farm last year over its âWild Rumpus Avocadoâ organic food pouch. The productâs front label describes it as an âOrganic Fruit & Veggie Blend,â and its ingredients are pineapple, banana, apple, avocado and mint.

    Industry observers note that parashos pointed to the U.S. Food and Drug Administrationâs classifications of avocado as a fruit and mint as an herb, meaning the blend contains no actual vegetables. Seeking a class action, she argued that Once Upon a Farm was committing fraud and violating California consumer protection and false advertising laws.

    In early August, Chen granted the companyâs motion to dismiss, deeming Once Upon a Farmâs use of âveggieâ as not âliterally false or so unambiguously deceptive that a reasonable consumer would not be expected to check the back label.â Two weeks later, the Barack Obama appointee changed his mind and asked for additional briefing.

    Based on a 2024 Ninth Circuit decision, Whiteside v. Kimberly Clark Corp, Chen found that Parashosâ claim of misrepresentation is viable.

    ââFruit & Veggie Blendâ is not a âmeaningless marketing termâ that the consumer would necessarily need more information to understand," he wrote.

    “The very fact that a reasonable consumer could reasonably conclude that the product contains a vegetable other than avocados is sufficient to state a claim of falsity without requiring consumers to read the back label,” he added.

    Chen denied Parashosâ request to enjoin Once Upon a Farm from marketing the product in the same way but allowed her claim for punitive damages and push for a class action to proceed.

    Once Upon a Farm did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.
    • The court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v.
    • Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    The court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services tech giant violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    The research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    Recent findings suggest that thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    Sources indicate that in June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    According to recent reports, in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    According to recent reports, however, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    Sources indicate that in August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    In a recent development, in their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    In a recent development, khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    After the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they said, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    The Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the issue at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    Recent findings suggest that in rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Upcoming York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    Recent findings suggest that maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at glitch in this case, the state remarked, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    Industry observers note that in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    According to recent reports, strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At glitch in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    It has been revealed that gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    And in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    Sources indicate that in its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Fresh York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    It has been revealed that the United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    In a recent development, justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

Graham, holding that a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause because it “has no secular legislative purpose.” That 1980 ruling is back in the spotlight this term, as the court considers whether to take up challenges to similar Ten Commandments laws in Texas and Louisiana.

    #20641. Industry News: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1886 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause.
    • According to recent reports, at the oral argument in St.
    • Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

    According to recent reports, at the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

    St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

    Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”.

    St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free exercise of religion as it requires them to accept students whose families do not adhere to the Catholic Church’s teachings, including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. The federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law.

    The 10th Circuit stressed that the Colorado law did not discriminate on the basis of religion. The court applied the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the free exercise clause cannot be used to challenge a neutral law of general applicability. This means that the free exercise clause is not a basis for an exception to a law unless it can be shown either that it was motivated by a desire to interfere with religion, that it discriminates against religion, or even that it just creates discretion to treat religions differently from secular actions. The 10th Circuit found that the Colorado law met the requirements for a neutral law of general applicability, as, among other things, it did not treat any one religion differently than others.

    According to recent reports, the court of appeals also found no discrimination against religious schools in government funding. In 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, the court declared unconstitutional a Missouri law that provided public and secular private schools funds for surfacing playgrounds that did not provide the same funds to religious schools. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, the court applied this to invalidate a Maine law that provided funds to parents to send their children to secular private schools in areas without public schools, but not “sectarian” schools. The 10th Circuit distinguished these cases, explaining that the Colorado law did not exclude religious schools as it allowed them to receive state money on the same terms as all other preschools.

    It has been revealed that at the oral argument on Nov. 3, there was more focus on the latter problem, perhaps because it would avoid the court needing to decide whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a concurring opinion, expressing support for that view, but finding it unnecessary to decide the issue to resolve that case. The court likely remains divided over whether to overrule Smith and what would replace it.

    Industry observers note that in the arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there were many questions from the conservative justices that suggested that they saw the Colorado law as discriminatory because of its effects on religious schools. For example, Chief Justice John Roberts asked the attorney for Colorado how this was different from the program in Carson v. Makin and said that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here,” as it disadvantaged religious schools. Barrett asked Colorado’s attorney why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can nevertheless “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows such “schools will be unable to agree to.”.

    In other words, these justices suggested that a discriminatory effect of Colorado’s law would be sufficient to find the law violated the free exercise of religion even though the law stated nothing about religion and was not motivated by a desire to interfere with religion. The questions suggested that Colorado adopting the non-discrimination requirement knowing that some religious schools would not comply should be sufficient to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause.

    It has been revealed that such an approach would be dramatically different from analysis under the equal protection clause. Although I personally think such cases were incorrectly decided, the Supreme Court long has held that proof of a discriminatory effect alone is not sufficient to establish race or sex discrimination. And it has expressly held that discrimination cannot be proven by showing that government officials took an action with knowledge that it would have discriminatory consequences.

    Industry observers note that washington v. Davis, decided 50 years ago, was a key case holding that a racially discriminatory effect is not sufficient to establish an equal protection violation. Applicants for the police force in Washington, D.C., were required to take a test, and statistics revealed that Black individuals failed the examination much more often than Whites. The Supreme Court, however, held that proof of a discriminatory impact is insufficient, by itself, to show the existence of a racial classification. Justice Byron White, writing for the majority, noted that the court never had held that “a law or other official act, without regard to whether it reflects a racially discriminatory purpose, is unconstitutional solely because it has a racially disproportionate impact.” The court explained that discriminatory impact, “[s]tanding alone, . . . does not trigger the rule that racial classifications are to be subjected to the strictest scrutiny and are justifiable only by the weightiest of considerations.”.

    According to recent reports, the court has even held that discriminatory purpose cannot be proven by showing that government officials adopted a policy with knowledge that it would have a discriminatory effect. Rather, the court has made it clear that showing such a purpose requires proof that the government desired to discriminate. In 1979’s Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts v. Feeney, the court declared: “‘Discriminatory purpose,’ … implies more than intent as volition or intent as awareness of consequences. It implies that the decisionmaker . . . selected or reaffirmed a particular course of action at least in part ‘because of,’ not merely ‘in spite of,’ its adverse effects upon an identifiable group.”.

    Feeney involved a challenge to a Massachusetts law that gave preference in hiring for state jobs to veterans. At the time of the litigation, more than 98% of the veterans in the state were male, and only 1.8% were female. The result was a substantial discriminatory effect against women in hiring for state jobs. Nonetheless, based on the principles articulated above, the Supreme Court held that there was not a sex classification because the law creating a preference for veterans was facially sex neutral and there was not proof that the state’s purpose in adopting the law was to disadvantage women. The fact that the legislature knew there would be an discriminatory effect against women was thus irrelevant.

    There is no way to reconcile this equal protection jurisprudence with the approach several conservative justices suggested in St. Mary Catholic Parish. The question then becomes whether there is any reason to treat discrimination under the free exercise clause differently from under the equal protection clause.

    In a recent development, several justices suggested in their questions at oral argument that Sherbet v. Verner, a 1963 case, justifies concluding that discriminatory impact is alone sufficient for a free exercise violation. That case involved a state having denied unemployment benefits to a woman, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, who quit her job rather than work on her Saturday Sabbath. The court concluded that the denial of benefits imposed a substantial burden on religion; the woman had to choose between an income and her faith. The court thus said that the concern was “whether some compelling state interest enforced in the eligibility provisions of the . . . statute justifies the substantial infringement of appellant’s First Amendment right.” The court found no such compelling interest and ruled that the denial of benefits constituted a violation of the free exercise clause.

    Sherbert found a violation of the free exercise of religion based on the impact on her religion despite the law at issue being facially neutral. As a precedent for striking down the Colorado law, however, that is unpersuasive. Sherbert was decided a decade before the Supreme Court held that proof of discriminatory impact was not sufficient for an equal protection violation. And although the court has not overruled Sherbert, it has never explained how it can be reconciled with Employment Division v. Smith. But most importantly, invoking Sherbert begs the crucial question: Should a different standard be used for discrimination under the free exercise clause compared to the equal protection clause?

    Conceptually, I cannot understand any reason why discrimination on the basis of religion should be treated dissimilarly from discrimination based on race or sex. Why should two such critical rights be treated differently? Indeed, it is just a doctrinal accident that religious discrimination is litigated under the free exercise clause (or the establishment clause) rather than the equal protection clause.

    Applying equal protection principles, the Colorado law does not discriminate against religion in its terms or in its purpose. Many commentators, including me, have argued that – despite court precedent – discriminatory impact should be enough for a claim under equal protection. But there has been no suggestion from the court that it is moving in that direction.

    Finally, it is important to stress that even if the law is deemed discriminatory, that does not mean that it is automatically unconstitutional. It means that strict scrutiny should be applied, in which the government action can be upheld if there is a compelling purpose for it. I was disappointed that the conservative justices did not focus on the government’s compelling interest in preventing children from being discriminated against on account of their gender identity or for having LGBTQ parents. Without explicitly saying so, the justices appear poised to carve out a special place for the free exercise clause over that of equal protection.

    Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

    Recommended Citation: Erwin Chemerinsky, Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 17, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/treating-the-free-exercise-of-religion-and-equal-protection-differently/.

    Recent findings suggest that viant bought Waymark this week. The deal will allow its marketer clients, especially small and midsize businesses (SMBs), make CTV ads that are better, cheaper and regularly refreshed.

    On today’s podcast, we discuss why time-strapped SMB marketers, who often lag enterprise marketers in tech adoption, have bucked the trend and become early adopters of AI. Business flyers, for example, are increasingly made by AI and promoted on Meta.     Then, we dissect The Trade Desk’s most recent earnings. Investors rewarded TTD with a 20% rise in stock price for having (almost) stabilizing revenue, which declined just $3 million to $736 million year over year. The Trade Desk touted that its strength in attracting political advertising and healthcare advertising, though it’s notable that the DSP’s rivals don’t play deeply in those highly regulated verticals. Amazon outright bans political advertising (though perhaps because Amazon operates a pharmacy, it’s open to healthcare and pharma ads, albeit with standard caveats), while Google tightly restricts both political and healthcare advertising.

    As part of its turnaround, it’s possible The Trade Desk may buy another organization, which it’s done only sparingly during its run as a DSP (Sincera being a notable exception). CEO Jeff Green signaled his openness to buying a company on the Q3 earnings call. Who knows what startups or established companies might call TTD in response.

    #20636. Latest Update: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1572 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    Section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    According to recent reports, as for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, said fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    The Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    But a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    In a recent development, for now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    Recent findings suggest that the 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, Fresh Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    In a recent development, if the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    In a recent development, that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process problem. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    According to recent reports, rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    CTV Has Trust Issues

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Around four months ago, a top ad sales executive at a CTV ad platform had a meeting with a large QSR advertiser, and he offered the CMO a guarantee.
    • “We stated, ‘You only pay us based on incremental visits to your store as defined and measured by your independent third-party measurement provider,’” the exec shared during a session at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit earlier this week, in what felt a little like group therapy for CTV ad tech platforms.
    • The QSR advertiser wasn’t convinced.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around four months ago, a top ad sales executive at a CTV ad platform had a meeting with a large QSR advertiser, and he offered the CMO a guarantee.

    “We stated, ‘You only pay us based on incremental visits to your store as defined and measured by your independent third-party measurement provider,’” the exec shared during a session at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit earlier this week, in what felt a little like group therapy for CTV ad tech platforms.

    Sounds like a slam dunk, right?

    Not so much. The QSR advertiser wasn’t convinced. “Well, how do I know I can trust them?” he apparently asked.

    “They’re your measurement partner!” the CTV ad exec recalled thinking, still incredulous in his retelling.

    “That’s when I gave up,” he mentioned.

    This tale highlights a frustration that plenty of CTV sellers share. They’ve spent years positioning connected TV as a vehicle for driving outcomes, not just reach and frequency – but getting advertisers to believe it is another matter.

    “We’re not there yet,” the CTV exec stated. “The promise is there, we’re pitching it, we have it, but we need advertisers to come on board.”.

    An ad industry vet – and self-described “recovering marketer” – in the audience piped up to venture a theory. It’s partially a perception thing.

    Although there’s been an “inexorable pull down the funnel” toward performance, he noted, marketers still tend to see TV as upper-funnel “hero media,” he said.

    It has been revealed that advertisers also often don’t have the right creative for CTV, and making the creative is too expensive. “There are legacy barriers to taking full advantage,” the vet remarked, “and [CTV is] just not seen as being as performative as programmatic.”.

    But whatever it is that’s holding buyers back, it’s not a lack of measurement options.

    The CEO and co-founder of a well-known CTV ad platform remarked that around 10 years ago when he started his firm, people would look at him cross-eyed when he tried to talk about incrementality.

    Recent findings suggest that but today, there are lots of different independent third-party measurement companies that offer incrementality through a variety of models. It’s a good thing, the CEO said.

    Recent findings suggest that yet, be that as it may, even the offer of a guarantee backed by independent measurement couldn’t close the deal for that aforementioned CTV ad exec. And sometimes the skepticism is warranted. There’s no denying that attribution is kind of a mess.

    Every channel, from display to social, tries to take credit for the same conversion, stated the co-founder and chief product officer of a streaming ad insertion platform.

    To be fair, CTV is no different in that regard, although it does bring something to the table that other channels don’t.

    “You’re getting a higher rate of attention,” the co-founder stated. “Yes, you might be paying more for it, but you need exposure and attention in order to actually convert.”.

    But it’s also worth pointing out that this whole debate can sound rather academic to the people who control the budgets, an executive on the buy side reminded the room.

    It has been revealed that “Not many brands think about all the things that we talk about on a daily basis,” mentioned the exec, who knows of what he speaks. Before joining a buy-side platform, he spent years as a marketer in media and strategy roles, including for a large candy brand.

    Marketers care about things like timing, seasonality and sales, not the ad tech plumbing underneath. And that, the exec argued, is why it makes sense for the DSP, not the publisher, to have the final say on when and where ads run across CTV and everywhere else.

    For example, October is like the Super Bowl for a large candy brand, but most candy sales don’t happen until the last three or four days of the month in the countdown to Halloween. When the exec would buy direct from publishers, however, most of the impressions would run in the first week of October, well before shoppers were thinking about Halloween candy, because the publishers were focused on monetizing their own inventory, not his business problems.

    There would only be a trickle of impressions remaining by the end of the month.

    If pressed, the exec said, “[the publishers] would be like, ‘Well, we delivered in full, what do you mean?”.

    “But I wanted 95% of my spend to be the last week of October,” he stated, “because it would have driven a lot more revenue for my company, not somebody else’s.”.

    Earning trust, it turns out, takes more than just a third-party measurement partner.
