    Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the mobile growth marketing platform reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on Thursday after the market closed.
    • Industry observers note that liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, up from $179.5 million during the same period last year.
    • Liftoff is pitching itself to Wall Street as riding two tailwinds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the mobile growth marketing platform reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on Thursday after the market closed. Shares were up by almost 25% overnight after the tech giant exceeded its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook moving forward.

    Industry observers note that liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, up from $179.5 million during the same period last year. And Liftoff delivered what investors really like to see: It earned $86.7 million in profit in the quarter, after taking a $5.7 million loss in Q3 a year ago.

    Liftoff is pitching itself to Wall Street as riding two tailwinds.

    There’s the overall growth of the mobile economy, to which the manufacturer’s growth is pegged; that growth is being boosted by an influx of AI-generated apps.

    And, secondly, there are the outsized revenue gains Liftoff earns through AI advancement compared to the relatively low investment the firm must shell out for AI and data infrastructure.

    It has been revealed that LLMs are great at coding apps and are thus “lowering the barrier” for companies or individuals to churn out a serviceable app, Liftoff CEO Jeremy Bondy told investors. “In the first half of this year alone, fresh apps released in the Apple App Store doubled versus the prior year to roughly 560,000.”.

    Recent findings suggest that each of these fresh apps has its own demand for new users. “For Liftoff, that means more demand for user acquisition,” Bondy mentioned.

    AI products are also separately “changing where search and discovery starts” for consumers, he stated.

    For one thing, that means “answering more questions without sending people to a website,” Bondy said. And that latest dynamic – where the open web is no longer a reliable traffic and user acquisition vehicle – incentivizes businesses to invest more into their own apps, where they still can “build direct relationships with their customers,” he added.

    AI search isn’t the only thing putting pressure on the open web when it comes to user acquisition. Apple’s iOS 27 machinations are also a drag on cross-site user tracking.

    AppLovin, which reported earnings a week ago, remarked that Apple’s obscure initiative to stamp out web tracking for all iOS devices will shift marketing budgets from the mobile web to mobile apps.

    And Bondy added some color, arguing that the mobile app advertising market is “drastically under-monetized” right now at about seven cents per hour, in terms of average earnings per attention time. That’s less than a sixth of what TV earns. Which means plenty of room for growth.

    Speaking of growth opportunities, there is also the fact that mobile marketing gains have, to date, mostly accrued to mobile gaming apps, Bondy said.

    Gaming is a category dominated by AppLovin, which is about 40x times bigger than Liftoff, in terms of the market cap. But more than half of Liftoff’s business is outside gaming, according to Bondy.

    Gaming apps are a valuable source of data, though, in regard to whether someone will actually fork over money when they’re using an app (rather than just being blasted by ads without making a purchase).

    “Someone who spends money in a game is also a potential high-value customer for a retailer, a social media app or a streaming service,” he said. And those are the categories in which Liftoff is positioned to grow, he said, as AppLovin has in the gaming space.

    However, those nongaming apps are more prone to seasonal fluctuations than gaming apps. Which can be a good or bad thing, depending on how revenue is currently ebbing and flowing.

    For instance, Liftoff rode the momentum from the FIFA World Cup and is seeing a similar surge for the NFL season, as advertisers are investing more in live sports. But it’s like surfing waves as they come, rather than riding a predictable cycle of consumer engagement ups and downs.

    But Bondy noted that Liftoff has been able to convert periodic or event-based customers (like a marketer investing in promoting their app around the World Cup) into steadier, higher-spending accounts.

    It has been revealed that liftoff had 396 customers who spent more than $100,000 in the past 12 months, Bondy stated. That’s up from 362 customers at the same time last year.

    Another key factor from the investor perspective is that Liftoff benefits from the AI revolution without having to financially support it.

    Bondy noted Liftoff has been able to greatly refine its ad targeting and personalization on the back of AI advances. The models are better at identifying a major spender from a retailer app, which makes that user a more valuable target in a gaming app, for example.

    Recent findings suggest that the models also now have greater longitudinal data, so they’re better at understanding long-term trends and how ROI develops over a year or more. However, the campaign returns from the week immediately after the budgets are spent are still the most vital data for the model’s decision-making, Bondy mentioned.

    Meanwhile, he added, Liftoff’s profit margin expansion in the past year was propelled by the company’s relatively low cost of infrastructure and AI services. The company’s entire capital expenditures (which encompass AI and data infrastructure costs) for Q3 was $14 million, or approximately 6% of revenue.

    In contrast, some companies that Liftoff competes with in mobile performance marketing (namely, Meta and Google) have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to their capex expenses.

    “As a reminder, our business is capital light,” Bondy told investors yesterday – and he periodically reminded them of this fact throughout the call.

    In a recent development, bondy also reminded investors that Liftoff will be discontinuing its reporting of “Core Advertising” revenue going forward because advertising is now almost the entirety of the tech giant’s business. And Liftoff has dropped the other (more expensive and subscription software-based) parts of its business, like a mobile ad network (perhaps you recall Vungle, which turned into Liftoff five years ago), and game developer analytics toolkit (an acquisition of GameRefinery).

    It has been revealed that liftoff’s Core Advertising revenue segment earned $237 million of the firm’s $237.5 in total earnings for Q3. Which illustrates why it no longer sees any need to break ads out as a separate line item.

    And Bondy sees nothing but green fields ahead for AI-optimized advertising.

    “Broadening the horizons in which we’re optimizing for our advertisers,” he stated, “there is just a tremendous amount of space for us to continue to grow this business.”.

    #20629. Significant Brands Have Forgotten How To Advertise; How Many Ads Can A Chatbot Chuck?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (814 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Significant Brands Have Forgotten How To Advertise; How Many Ads Can A Chatbot Chuck?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Many of the best-known, most-loved, classic Americana brands are stagnant, if not on the decline.
    • The Trade Desk Co-Founder and CEO Jeff Green opines on that painful, unacknowledged reality in a column for The Current, TTD’s news and content marketing site.
    • Green points out that AT&T, Gap, General Mills, Clorox, Best Buy, Coca-Cola, Macy’s, Nike, Pepsi, Campbell’s, Procter & Gamble, Kroger, Ford, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Verizon and many more such examples have lagged behind US GDP growth in recent years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Many of the best-known, most-loved, classic Americana brands are stagnant, if not on the decline.

    The Trade Desk Co-Founder and CEO Jeff Green opines on that painful, unacknowledged reality in a column for The Current, TTD’s news and content marketing site.

    Green points out that AT&T, Gap, General Mills, Clorox, Best Buy, Coca-Cola, Macy’s, Nike, Pepsi, Campbell’s, Procter & Gamble, Kroger, Ford, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Verizon and many more such examples have lagged behind US GDP growth in recent years.

    Only the very biggest companies in their categories have exceeded GDP growth. As in, Walmart is fine, but not even Target is hitting the mark.

    Green focuses his analysis on the consumer side, but he could also point to American media brands. Studio empires have crumbled or confederated, while even a standout like Disney is still flat. The Upcoming York Times persists, but once-legendary news and magazine businesses are barely getting by.

    The oxygen has partly been sucked out of the brand economy by the growth of Meta, Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

    But Green’s focus is actually internal to the brands, not factors outside their control. These classic companies are “not growing in part because they don’t brand-build like they once did,” he writes.

    Marketers must rediscover their own lost art. Which Green describes as “using memory structures created through experiences (usually ads) that make people feel something.”.

    Google’s Q3 earnings caused its stock to tank after the company admitted it’s not showing as many ads in AI search as it did in traditional search.

    However, Google’s gambit is laying the groundwork for “an engagement sink” in which its Gemini chatbot and AI Overviews can “serve an ad each time the user submits a follow-up question,” writes Eric Seufert at Mobile Dev Memo.

    Although, as Seufert also points out, that will require a lot of complicated calculations to determine how often to show ads without causing the user to bounce.

    Recent findings suggest that it makes sense to use each subsequent user input as data for refining the ad targeting. But if you’re blasting the user with ads each time they enter an input, the experience is no better than those 50-page chumbox slideshows that refresh the ads every time you press “Next.”.

    Industry observers note that seufert takes an admirable crack at trying to formulate an equation for when the diminishing returns from sharper ad targeting get offset by the increasing likelihood of the user bouncing. It’s the kind of heady stuff that could make even the most hardened ad tech engineer’s eyes glaze over – but also the kind of math problem AI is allegedly equipped to tackle.

    Still, it’s ironic that now Google finds itself in the same position as cash-strapped publishers: trying to figure out how many ads they can cram into an interaction before the user goes running.

    Twitch is opening up to short-form videos created outside the platform, plus fresh paid media opportunities to turn those clips into a discovery vehicle on Twitch itself.

    According to recent reports, but don’t just call it another TikTok copycat. Or, as Twitch product chief Mike Minton put it on stage at the TwitchCon 2026 event in San Diego last week, “We’re not trying to be TwitchTok,” Digiday reports.

    In a recent development, it is a unique situation for the livestreamed video-gaming platform. Twitch was actually early to the clipping trend. It has long had a “Clips” tab for its content creators to do their own clipping and editing from their streams. That way, they can cut hourslong livestreams into short-form videos that would routinely blow up on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, etc.

    However, Minton said, Twitch had “missed an opportunity” to make the clipping phenomenon a thing on Twitch.

    So, will Twitch viewers watch viral TikTok posts, even of their favorite streamers? Maybe.

    But there are other benefits for Twitch.

    “It sounds like they’re trying to capture more inventory as leverage from an advertising perspective,” says Justin Miclat, chief growth officer at talent and brand management manufacturer Click Media.

    ChatGPT launches a wallet feature that allows customers to make purchases with an AI agent. [WSJ].

    According to recent reports, AI is turning ad tech into a fight for the brain behind the buy. [Digiday].

    Industry observers note that roughly 60 SpaceX employees who worked on Grok Imagine, the company’s AI video and image generation tool, were laid off this week. [The Information].

    It has been revealed that google had a $1.7 billion fine for anticompetitive search advertising practices called off in 2019. But a higher court ruling now might tack that fine back onto Google’s bill. [Reuters].

    Recent findings suggest that A Google Ads patch makes it easier for advertisers to provide detailed technical requirements for incrementality studies. [Search Engine Roundtable].

    #20625. Most Retail Media Networks Shouldn’t Exist. Here’s How They Can Prove Their Worth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (808 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Most Retail Media Networks Shouldn’t Exist. Here’s How They Can Prove Their Worth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We’re well past the point of oversaturation in ad tech.
    • Sources indicate that there are more than 175,000 software vendors listed on G2, over 15,000 marketing technology solutions and reportedly over 12,000 ad tech vendors in operation.
    • According to recent reports, but no tech market is more ripe for consolidation than retail media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’re well past the point of oversaturation in ad tech.

    Sources indicate that there are more than 175,000 software vendors listed on G2, over 15,000 marketing technology solutions and reportedly over 12,000 ad tech vendors in operation. Competitive intensity is real.

    According to recent reports, but no tech market is more ripe for consolidation than retail media. Look no further than DoorDash’s recent $17 billion acquisition of Instacart. And then there’s Kevel, which supplies ad technology infrastructure to retail media networks and  recently raised $52 million. Its founder and CEO, James Avery, told AdExchanger that a lot of retail media companies are selling to the same customers and that “consolidation is going to happen.”.

    He also stated Kevel likes to joke that “we’re going to help launch 1,000 walled gardens, but then the brands are, like, ‘No, please don’t!’”.

    Industry observers note that the brands are right. For many, the media network model is the wrong bet to make.

    According to recent reports, amazon and Walmart took 85.5% of US retail media spend in 2025, leaving only 14.5% for every other network, combined. EMarketer expects this duopoly to take 89% of the growth in 2026 and the share held by every other network it tracks to stay flat or fall through 2027.

    According to recent reports, brands haven’t stopped adding networks to their looks, though. McKinsey found that a third of US advertisers used nine or more commerce media networks in 2025. But the reality is that a network can appear on a media blueprint and still receive very little of the budget.

    The same McKinsey survey found that as advertisers add networks, their audiences overlap and the networks become harder to pull apart. Ad buyers told eMarketer much the same thing: They struggle to distinguish one platform from another. The retailer’s brand just isn’t enough of a differentiator.

    Too many networks exist without addressing the biggest question: “Why should I be chosen?” Most networks are selling to the same brands and addressing the same audiences, while describing themselves with the same claims about first-party purchasing data and closed-loop measurement. As such, buyers have nothing to base their choice on except for scale and price. And no one beats Amazon there.

    The untapped opportunity is for retailers to differentiate their measurement stacks.

    In a recent development, in NIQ’s CMO Outlook survey, 67% of CMOs noted they planned to increase spending on retail media networks in 2026. Yet only 53% believe today’s networks provide adequate measurement and attribution.

    Retailers want to see why each decision in an auction was made: “It’s not enough to say, ‘Trust us, this is doing the best it can for you,’” Kevel’s Avery told AdExchanger.

    Recent findings suggest that advertisers are asking for the same evidence. A brand that can’t compare results across networks will most likely keep its budget where the results are easiest to read.

    Sources indicate that A retailer’s own shopper data is the one asset no other network can copy. It’s proprietary and unique by definition. But siloing this advantage behind a separate walled login is an expensive and high-friction way of realizing value.

    Some retailers have started selling shopper data through partnerships and tools that brands can more easily access.

    Tesco, B&Q, John Lewis and Waitrose are piloting dunnhumby’s network alliance, which gives brands a single way to run a campaign across several retailers, with shared standards for measurement and reporting.

    Kevel has built API access with Pacvue and Skai along with an integration that lets brands buying Dollar General’s off-site ads through The Trade Desk buy its on-site ads the same way.

    In both cases, the retailer still runs its own media business, but brands don’t have to learn its system to buy from it.

    Sources indicate that avery expects consolidation among the infrastructure vendors that sell to and support retailers, and Kevel now has the money to win that fight. But advertisers will inevitably consolidate their media looks as well. WARC forecasts that, outside Amazon, global retail media growth will slow to 9.8% in 2027. That’s the lowest rate since it began tracking the market. When growth slows, brands will remove the networks they can’t tell apart or can’t compare on performance.

    Sources indicate that in 2027, every retail media network will have to answer three questions from the advertisers and agencies it sells to. Why should we choose you over Amazon? Can you prove what our media investment did and compare that to other networks? Can we use familiar tools to buy on your network?

    Those who can answer all three questions stand the best chance of being part of the media strategy next year.

    “Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

    Follow Paul Evans and AdExchanger on LinkedIn.

    The Marketing Team at OpenZeppelin drives awareness and adoption across every product and service we ship, from the flagship OpenZeppelin Contracts Libraries to security audits, developer tooling, and solutions for financial institutions.

    Working hand-in-hand with Product, Design, Sales, and Open Source Engineering, the team owns messaging, go-to-market strategy, content, and events that position OpenZeppelin as the security standard for onchain finance.

    As OpenZeppelin’s Senior Product Marketer for Financial Services, you will own how we position, launch, and sell our solutions to banks, asset managers, and financial market infrastructures. You will lead the go-to-market for new institutional solutions, from positioning through launch and adoption, and make sure Sales has what it needs to win. You will work AI-native by default: building the workflows, agents, and tools that let you research faster, create better content, and give Sales assets that adapt to every account instead of going stale.

    #20623. Ad Tech Is Getting Better At Fixing Its Flaws Instead Of Just Calling Them Out, Says DecryptAds’ Latest COO Arielle Garcia

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1308 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Ad Tech Is Getting Better At Fixing Its Flaws Instead Of Just Calling Them Out, Says DecryptAds’ Latest COO Arielle Garcia

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Constantly pointing out that a system is broken gets old.
    • Sources indicate that arielle Garcia has been one of digital advertising’s most outspoken voices advocating for the need for better data privacy and cybersecurity for the past decade, going back to her work as a compliance manager and chief privacy officer for ad agency UM Worldwide.
    • Now, she’s taking on a new role as chief operating officer for advertising cybersecurity startup DecryptAds, the company revealed Monday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Constantly pointing out that a system is broken gets old. Eventually, you just want to roll up your sleeves and fix it yourself.

    Sources indicate that arielle Garcia has been one of digital advertising’s most outspoken voices advocating for the need for better data privacy and cybersecurity for the past decade, going back to her work as a compliance manager and chief privacy officer for ad agency UM Worldwide. And after leaving UM in 2023, she joined ad industry watchdog group Check My Ads and introduced her own ad tech accountability consultancy.

    Now, she’s taking on a new role as chief operating officer for advertising cybersecurity startup DecryptAds, the company revealed Monday. And Garcia told AdExchanger she believes this will be her most consequential role yet in building a better ad tech industry for advertisers and consumers. In addition to overseeing DecryptAds’ day-to-day operations, she’ll be leading its industry partnerships and engagement with brands, standards bodies and lawmakers.

    DecryptAds was launched this summer by cybersecurity and privacy researcher Zach Edwards, whose work Garcia mentioned she’s been following since her days at UM. Garcia and Edwards also worked together at Check My Ads, where Garcia was COO and Edwards served as a board member until 2025.

    DecryptAds is building what Edwards describes as his “dream research tool for understanding and tracking publishers and ad systems.”.

    The firm’s goal, Garcia noted, is to give researchers, ad agencies, tech companies, industry groups and regulators the evidence they need to identify and fix security gaps in the programmatic supply chain.

    According to recent reports, decryptAds examines publicly available data, including ads.txt and sellers.json files, to determine the entities behind publisher sites and ad tech vendors. And it flags when those entities have ties to regions that are sanctioned by the US government or that have high degrees of cybercrime and lax data security practices.

    The company is also rolling out a service for notifying clients when other ad systems drop sellers and publishers by examining sellers.json files and tracking API and MCP connections. The service should aid the endless “wack-a-mole” game ad tech vendors have to play to keep their supply chains clean, Garcia said.

    She spoke to AdExchanger about promoting industry change through better collaboration in her upcoming role.

    AdExchanger: Why join DecryptAds?

    ARIELLE GARCIA: The most powerful work that I’ve been a part of is where we take information and bring it to both the market and to government to help inform better decisions or support investigations or lawmaking. For example, when Check My Ads did our Google PMAX research, it wasn’t just a primer on watchouts for small businesses or education for nonprofits. It helped support lawmakers making the case for why regulation wouldn’t break online advertising.

    So, when Zach reached out about joining DecryptAds, I was thrilled because what the team is building here is founded on getting information and evidence into everyone’s hands.

    You’ve covered how hard it can be for watchdogs to get access to the systems that they’re trying to hold accountable. DecryptAds doesn’t depend on anyone’s permission. It’s built from public data, the files companies are publishing and the infrastructure behind their sites.

    In your hiring announcement, you said “After years of identifying the problems in the ad tech ecosystem, I’m proud to be joining a tech giant that’s building a solution.” Does it feel like the industry is getting better at fixing its vulnerabilities rather than just constantly raising the alarm?

    The appetite for making this data available is something that’s been growing for a couple of years. We’ve seen this increasingly with the great work Confiant, DeepSee and Adalytics have done.

    Sources indicate that I’ve had the opportunity to refine my theory of change a bit. There’s an important role for those who are calling out the problems, and there’s an important role for those who are building solutions to fix them. Not everyone is positioned to do both.

    But I enjoy working with the industry. And I see changing market behavior as an key lever for improving the industry for marketers, the public and for national security. For me personally, [this role] is an evolution of where I think I can be the most useful.

    Will DecryptAds’ research be mainly focused on ad tech cybersecurity or programmatic supply-chain quality? Or are those two inextricably related?

    The security framing demonstrates up in how our tool enables the tracing of networks. So understanding that MFA [made-for-advertising] operators and bad actors will try to hide and building that into our capabilities.

    In a recent development, but the security ethos also highlights up in the spirit of information sharing. That’s why the product has a free researcher tier. Having come from a watchdog organization, I’m excited about giving access to this information to researchers that are presently lacking ways to dig deep into the ecosystem.

    According to recent reports, it’s been a bad couple of weeks for ad tech cybersecurity news. Are things getting worse, or are they getting easier to catch?

    Right, on top of the recent AdFection report by Confiant and Citizen Lab, there’s the military warning that ad data was used to target troops. Also fairly recently, the DOJ bulk data transfer rule. Now you have senators calling for reform in the wake of AdFection.

    In a recent development, the government has known for years that ads can be an attack surface. The NSA, CISA and FBI all recommend ad blocking since 2018. But where it used to be more about blocking malicious ads, now there’s more of a realization of the ad system itself being a national security risk.

    What’s one way the digital ad industry can work with regulators and researchers to support a safer, more transparent supply chain?

    There’s fairly broad recognition of the need for stronger Know Your Customer standards for ad tech. It gets at the core of so many of the scandals that we’ve seen happen over the past few years. And yet trade associations, independent companies and standards bodies aren’t truly embracing the spirit behind that.

    How would better Know Your Customer standards work in practice?

    DecryptAds has seen how valuable it is to have some type of a geo risk score. It’s fairly easy to determine whether a vendor or a publisher is based in a high-risk or sanctioned jurisdiction. So it’s a strange miss on advertiser verification to not even verify the domain of the advertiser.

    And to not have a Know Your Customer vetting process be a part of what TAG [the Trustworthy Accountability Group] expects of certified vendors is surprising to me.

    What would you say to companies who might get defensive if they show up in your research?

    It’s about collaborating on solutions. It’s always been key to me to be fair and to have receipts. And the goal is never to call out one particular actor when you’re trying to fix a systemic problem. There’s nothing wrong with acknowledging the problem and sharing the steps you’re taking to fix it.

    One of the things that was shocking in the wake of the Confiant/Citizen Lab AdFection report was IAB Europe’s reaction, which was to say, the system’s not broken, but it can be exploited.

    I’ve been contending with some iteration of that narrative since I was an agency-side chief privacy officer. The system is broken. The system is able to easily be exploited, and actions are not being taken to close those gaps.

    According to recent reports, so accountability in the interest of benefiting everyone should be the goal. And it’s okay to make a mistake or to have an oversight. But it’s not okay to bury our collective heads in the sand as though these are just unfortunate, isolated incidents.

    This interview has been edited and condensed.

    #20620. Why Trade Desk Veteran Jed Dederick Joined The Startup ShopMy To Sell Creator Marketing

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1026 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Trade Desk Veteran Jed Dederick Joined The Startup ShopMy To Sell Creator Marketing

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry.
    • In a recent development, the rest, as they say, is history.
    • But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry. He was a digital ads seller first at The Wall Street Journal and then WebMD until 2012, when he jumped across the exchange to the still-nascent DSP The Trade Desk.

    In a recent development, the rest, as they say, is history. He eventually led all TTD sales as CRO, and had industry stage time as an expert witness throughout the Department of Justice’s publisher ad tech antitrust suit against Google.

    But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.

    “In a world where the older forms of performance marketing like search are seeing massive declines and are in huge question,” creator content is ready to step up, he told AdExchanger.

    We caught up with Dederick about the fresh role and how, practically speaking, social creator commerce can become an always-on paid performance channel.

    DEDERICK: I have lots of experience with how ads have funded the distribution of content and information. The thing that stood out to me was how crowded and commoditized paid advertising has become.

    [ShopMy] has this idea that there’s all of this value and performance locked up inside creator content. Brands see it with high conversion rates and success rates with individual creator relationships, but haven’t had real scale or measurability.

    According to recent reports, and I see a tremendous amount of untapped performance marketing value in the creator commerce world. I mean, for instance, if you’re interested in buying the best mosquito zapper, that’s easier now than it’s ever been.

    The process of discovery, inspiration and purchase is happening inside the creator landscape. And there are huge pockets of individual value that haven’t been tied together.

    How does the marketplace model work?

    On the brand side, it’s a subscription model.

    Recent findings suggest that anybody who’s worked on the brand side in creator influencer marketing knows it’s really painful to set up an individual relationship with a creator. The trade-off for that one relationship hasn’t always translated into a massive vehicle or a line item for performance marketing. And so what we’re doing is making it possible for a brand to reach thousands of valuable creators at once through one central place.

    Does ShopMy have its own app or is it only plugged into affiliate networks and places where products are sold?

    Industry observers note that our creators are putting up content in a lot of places [with affiliate marketing programs]. Meta is certainly one. Substack is one. TikTok is one. And understanding that creators have a lot of platforms to put out content, ShopMy is a central place for brands and creators.

    It has been revealed that traditionally, brands have had to go to multiple places to manage individual creator relationships or rely on platform reporting from all the different places those creators can be. [ShopMy] is an easy way to gain promotion by creators without having to create individual, unique sponsorships with the creators.

    And, I’ll also add, we’ve released a shopper app very recently.

    It has been revealed that we’re doing $1.9 billion in GMV [“gross merchandise volume,” for the uninitiated] right now. So I think part of why this probably isn’t in the lexicon is that [ShopMy] has lived a lot in the commerce landscape, particularly in fashion and beauty.

    According to recent reports, but you can see why I look at this from a performance marketing lens and think, “Oh my goodness! If only the brands that I know and have worked with could run this way and think this way. This doesn’t need to just live in one pocket of the ecosystem.”.

    Recent findings suggest that who are you dealing with at an advertiser client? The “affiliate person” in the marketing org could be very different from the “performance marketing person.”.

    Sources indicate that this is why I’m here. This is what I think is fun: busting up the old silos in the name of value and efficiency.

    I mentioned that we have thousands of premium brand partners, like Jimmy Choo, for the sake of example. Those types of brands have had creator teams and affiliate teams, right? Sometimes they sit under PR. Sometimes it’s under the umbrella of social or paid media.

    According to recent reports, brands have organized themselves that way because that’s been the opportunity so far. But what I do is I bring scale and liquidity that can make [creator content] basically a vehicle for what would have been performance marketing and paid media budgets.

    In terms of working with hundreds of thousands of creators – orthodontists, baristas, airline stewardesses and endlessly on – how are they selling general stuff?

    I think this idea is so much bigger than it currently is.

    Recent findings suggest that people’s social circles are how we’ve gotten trusted recommendations forever. Your friends or someone you trust in a field have given you recommendations, and those are way more powerful than anything you’ve gotten through paid ads.

    Industry observers note that there are people in our network across lots of disciplines who have their own followings in their fields. So, sure, in that case, that might be relevant for endemic brands. But an orthodontist might be relevant for oral care and personal care brands. Creators post lifestyle-oriented [content] across categories: be it travel, fashion, cosmetics.

    The reality of this landscape is how we get recommendations that used to be from our friends, maybe a co-worker, someone from a group chat. That’s the basis for what we’re scaling with creators.

    Is there a brand safety/verification-type partner?

    I had the same questions coming in.

    The reality is that how we think of user-generated and quote-unquote “premium” content is less helpful now. I don’t know about you, but when I go home, I turn on Netflix, and I see YouTube creators on Netflix. What my family’s watching is YouTube creators on Netflix with longer-format shows.

    The world has changed quite a bit. There’s authentic content that connects, and there’s everything else.

This is a hands-on role for someone who loves building secure systems and influencing security culture in a fast-paced fintech startup.

    You will act as a key advisor on secure architecture. You will own the work of identifying, fixing, and preventing vulnerabilities across our services, cloud environments, tooling, and developer workflows.

    The SecOps team is a focused group responsible for application security and cloud security across the product. We help Clutch scale securely and efficiently.

    We partner closely with product engineering to embed security throughout the SDLC.

    In a recent development, we value pragmatism, ownership, and curiosity. We always ask: “How can we make this safer and faster?”.

    We are building a security first engineering culture that enables teams to move fast and responsibly, without slowing them down.

    Assess our application and cloud security posture, and map the highest risks across services, cloud accounts, and pipelines.

    Embed with engineering teams to review security critical features and give practical guidance on secure design.

    Integrate developer friendly security tooling (SAST, SCA, secret scanning, IaC scanning) into our CI/CD pipelines.

    Triage and remediate early vulnerabilities, and set a baseline for secure coding and cloud hardening.

    Lead the design and rollout of a Secure SDLC with actionable security gates and clear ownership at each stage.

    Establish cloud security controls, including IAM least privilege, secrets management, and logging for threat detection.

    Build internal tooling to automate threat detection, cloud posture monitoring, and vulnerability management.

    Launch an internal security playbook with incident response runbooks tailored to Clutch’s tech stack.

    Develop and maintain secure libraries and frameworks used across engineering, such as auth modules and input validators.

    Drive continuous cloud security improvements through policy as code, automated compliance checks, and drift detection.

    Build and mentor a security champion network inside engineering teams.

    Partner with developers to threat model upcoming services and cloud architecture changes.

    5+ years of experience in software/application security, ideally in fast-growing startups or fintech environments.

    Deep knowledge of web application security, secure software design, API hardening, and threat modeling.

    Experience integrating security into CI/CD pipelines, including use of SAST, DAST, SCA, and IaC scanning tools.

    Familiarity with common compliance frameworks (e.g., SOC 2, GLBA, PCI-DSS) and cloud-native security (AWS, GCP preferred).

    Strong coding background (e.g., Node.js, Python, Go) and ability to read, understand, and debug code securely.

    Excellent communication skills, with the ability to influence without authority and foster cross-functional collaboration.

    Please note that this role may evolve as our business needs change, so we appreciate your flexibility and adaptability.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off and National Holidays: Enjoy 20 PTO days yearly and the National Holidays for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Going Straight To The C-Suite; All I Want For Christmas Is Hess Truck Ads In September

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pinch your nose and blow gently through your nostrils.
    • That’s how to unpop your eardrums on a plane, or after taking the elevator from the lowly marketer offices to the executive floor.
    • It has been revealed that earlier this month, this newsletter noted the trend of holdco CEOs making handshake deals with brand CEOs to poach accounts their agencies didn’t even pitch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pinch your nose and blow gently through your nostrils.

    That’s how to unpop your eardrums on a plane, or after taking the elevator from the lowly marketer offices to the executive floor.

    It has been revealed that earlier this month, this newsletter noted the trend of holdco CEOs making handshake deals with brand CEOs to poach accounts their agencies didn’t even pitch. That’s the theory behind Publicis landing PepsiCo, Microsoft and LVMH.

    Deloitte Digital is another example, as Digiday reports. The marketing consultancy arm of Deloitte’s holdco is going straight to CEOs to pitch its new enterprise operating system.

    It has been revealed that traditionally, the marketing department has been Deloitte’s target and entry point. But the kind of enterprise deal it’s now seeking requires CEO approval and is part of a “more executive conversation,” claims Deloitte Digital US CMO Mark Singer.

    Plus, Deloitte’s product is called Converge Front Office (or “CFO,” lol).

    The product name is fitting, as Gartner VP Jay Wilson perhaps unwittingly notes, since CFOs are taking bigger roles in evaluating marketing spend: “Increasingly, we see and hear from clients and agencies that the CFO is the critical piece of the fresh business puzzle, as marketing budgets remain flat.”.

    Sources indicate that deloitte Digital’s thinking is that brands have archives of back-filled content, copy and campaigns that haven’t been touched in ages. So why not have AI agents upcycle that content instead of buying more?

    Gotta hand it to them; it’s definitely not a holdco pitch.

    It’s not just you – the Christmas creep started creeping even earlier this year.

    This September, there were 11% more holiday-themed ads on TV than in 2025 and six times more than in 2021, according to Nielsen.

    Not surprisingly, retailers are on track to spend the most of any ad vertical. They made up almost 64% of all holiday ads aired on linear TV in October, which actually outpaces their usual holiday ad blitz. Over the past five years, retail accounted for about 45% of holiday ads across both linear and streaming TV.

    In a recent development, nielsen also notes some historical trends that could factor into this holiday season. For instance, there were a lot more automotive holiday ads on streaming (18.4%) than there were on linear (9.7%) last year. Maybe it’s a way to appeal to cord-cutting millennials who’ve started saying “Happy Honda Days” to each other as a bit.

    But does running holiday ads sooner get consumers to spend more throughout the season?

    It has been revealed that according to Deloitte’s annual holiday shopping survey (which was conducted between late August and early September), the average household spend will increase 4% to $1,654 this year. And, while 22% of consumers plan to shop earlier this year, they expect 28% of their budgets to be spent by the end of October – the highest share Deloitte has seen in six years.

    It has been revealed that so total holiday spending may be up a bit. But it won’t pay to wait until Mariah Carey is fully thawed to run those ads.

    Recent findings suggest that the global internet is getting less global. And questions that once seemed outright crazy – such as, “Might Meta stop doing business in the European Union?” – are not so crazy anymore.

    There’s no urgent crisis for Meta. The canary in the coal mine is really X. Elon Musk has threatened to stop serving X owners in Europe going back to 2023 and fumed over a $140 million Digital Services Act fine last year.

    But as Eric Seufert notes at Mobile Dev Memo, there’s a confluence of problems in Europe for Meta that could force its hand.

    Like X, Meta has also dealt with growing fines from EU regulators. Italy tagged it just yesterday with another billion or so in penalties over privacy violations involving scanned Android camera rolls.

    The EU’s anti-personalization rules and requirement that Meta offer an ad-free subscription service have also decreased the platform’s advertising payouts.

    Plus, the European Commission’s Digital Fairness Act is taking shape. It would prohibit common mobile game monetization tactics like offering virtual in-game currencies or letting consumers pay for “variable-reward systems” (aka loot boxes). If mobile games make less money in the EU, that means smaller budgets for mobile app advertising, which is a revenue pillar for Meta.

    At some point, these things add up. And, eventually, staying in the EU may not make mathematical sense for Meta.

    Recent findings suggest that hearst Magazines releases an agency-esque studio that pairs creators with its editorial brands and advertisers for original content and/or branded campaigns. [Adweek].

    Industry observers note that california sues OpenAI over the Hugging Face incident and other examples of AI agents overstepping their boundaries and escaping research environments. [release].

    Taboola completed its acquisition of Dianomi, a digital ad platform for business, financial services and lifestyle audiences. [release].

    Roughly one in five marketers are trying to quit their jobs – more than double the average for other white collar fields. [Adweek].

    In a recent development, first, email on Thursday, then flights on Friday … on Monday, it was banks reporting technical outages. [Newsweek].

    Websites Aren’t Just For People Anymore. Here’s How Marketers Optimize Them For Agents

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s always nice for a marketer to get a compliment on their website.
    • Ask again in a few months and we might have an answer.
    • On Tuesday, customer journey intelligence platform Knotch declared a new solution called Ace for Agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s always nice for a marketer to get a compliment on their website. But does the compliment still resonate when it comes from an AI agent?

    Ask again in a few months and we might have an answer.

    On Tuesday, customer journey intelligence platform Knotch declared a new solution called Ace for Agents. The product builds on its existing AI marketing solution, Ace, but is specifically focused on making website content more accessible to AI agents.

    But what does it mean for content to be accessible to agents that, by definition, can access pretty much all content across the web?

    Effectively, it involves reformatting content into simpler terms and unifying it from multiple sources onto a single webpage, noted Andrew Bolton, chief customer officer at Knotch.

    Sources indicate that most LLM crawlers declare themselves when they access a webpage, so Knotch knows to show them the AI version of a page, mentioned Bolton. For those that don’t declare, Ace can analyze actions like on-site behavior to determine that the viewer is a bot.

    Industry observers note that AI agents, unlike humans, don’t care about interactive features or aesthetically pleasing graphics. Instead, their focus is on brevity and direct statements.

    According to recent reports, often, the reformatting includes adding FAQs and concise summaries, as well as removing JavaScript. The result is a pared-down version of the webpage a human would see, but the key content remains.

    According to recent reports, that’s what Bolton describes as a one-to-one version of an existing webpage, in which the information that’s already on it is simply restructured, but nothing new is added. That’s one of the two types of pages that Ace for Agents can develop – the simpler, “v1” offering, said Bolton.

    The slightly more advanced version of Ace for Agents involves “injecting newly introduced components of information” from other sources of the brand’s choosing, he mentioned, like third-party review sites, or the brand’s own YouTube channel.

    For instance, he added, if a car manufacturer had a particularly favorable review on a third-party site comparing one of its models to a competitor’s model, Knotch can ingest that into the manufacturer’s context model.

    It has been revealed that reviews “would be valuable to a consumer who’s trying to evaluate those two different vehicles,” he added. Marketers have a say on whether they want to manually flag external reviews and other content to pull in, or if they want to use an agent to automatically pull in upcoming, positive content, which a human can then review.

    The resulting webpage is a “super piece of content” that is able to “combine the atoms” of several different pages across the web, mentioned Bolton. Now, an LLM only needs to access one page, but gets the same amount of data that it historically would’ve collected from crawling all of the data sources individually.

    It’s worth noting that the data inputs are entirely curated by the brand. In other words, the good reviews will be ingested, and the bad ones won’t. A brand wouldn’t elect to put negative reviews on their website, Bolton remarked, and Knotch is effectively creating an agent-readable webpage that pulls all of the informative and positive information on the brand into a single source.

    As marketing and the open web rapidly evolve, agencies need to build an “experience that reaches both the people and the machines,” Melissa Berger, chief solutions officer at Digitas, told AdExchanger. “Earning attention” has always been a major focus for the agency, Berger remarked, “and now that’s not just earning from the human; it’s earning from the agents, too.”.

    Digitas has been working with Knotch for over a year and began testing Ace for Agents several months ago as a way to earn some of that agentic attention.

    In a recent development, although Ace for Agents has been a good way for brands to increase discoverability, they still need to understand who their human customers are, mentioned Berger. Otherwise, the LLM-accessible site may be full of information, but not have the answers to the specific questions the humans are looking for.

    Once a brand understands exactly what sort of questions its customers are asking and what queries it should aim to show up against, mentioned Berger, “the rest of the content is updated to be catered more toward that.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After building brands alongside some of YouTube’s biggest kid-friendly stars, pocket.watch is increasing its presence in the world of film distribution. The creator media firm has come on board as the exclusive worldwide distributor and sales agent for Reef to Ridge, a nature documentary directed by Brave Wilderness Co-Founder and CEO Mark Vins.

    Reef to Ridge takes viewers to the Galapagos Islands, where Vins and his crew explore unique habitats, encounter endangered species, and discuss the challenges that hinder conservation efforts around the world. The project premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) where it was part of a showcase curated by YouTube. By highlighting projects from creators like Vins and Ziwe, YouTube showed that its biggest draws were ready for Hollywood close-ups.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, by working with Vins to give Reef to Ridge a streaming premiere, pocket.watch is solving a problem that has stunted progress for some creators with Hollywood ambitions. Major studios are eager to turn YouTube stars into feature directors, but the distributors attached to those projects have often been film industry firms like A24 and Neon. Meanwhile, creators who eschew traditional distribution can encounter some headaches, as Markiplier discovered when he attempted to bring his video game adaptation Iron Lung to YouTube.

    It has been revealed that as a creator media company, pocket.watch can pursue global distribution for a project like Reef to Ridge while also understanding the needs of a director like Vins. “Creators have built extraordinary relationships with their audiences, and there is a real opportunity to bring that connection to feature films,” noted pocket.watch Founder and CEO Chris M. Williams in a statement. “Mark Vins and his team have made a visually striking, cinematic film with the ambition and scale to reach well beyond their established fanbase. We’re bringing our distribution expertise and platform partnerships to that opportunity, with more creator-led film announcements to come.”.

    As Williams alluded to in his statement, Reef to Ridge is just the start for pocket.watch. The media firm is going to help creators realize their feature film ambitions. According to a press release, more announcements of this nature will arrive “by year’s end.”.

    #20611. Breaking: Ad Tech Doesn’t Need Another Tool. It Needs Fewer Handoffs

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (692 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Ad Tech Doesn’t Need Another Tool. It Needs Fewer Handoffs

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every few months, we get excited about an industry update, like a fresh ad format or AI tool.
    • Industry observers note that the marketing technology landscape has 15,384 solutions and counting.
    • Think about a typical day for an affiliate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every few months, we get excited about an industry update, like a fresh ad format or AI tool. That energy is a massive part of what keeps ad tech moving forward, but I believe the next five years will be shaped less by any single innovation and more by how well the tools we already have work together.

    Industry observers note that the marketing technology landscape has 15,384 solutions and counting. The opportunity now is in the gaps between them, because that’s where time, data and trust get lost.

    Think about a typical day for an affiliate. They usually juggle several platforms to find offers and buy traffic. And when it comes to site or landing-page monetization, that can mean yet another platform. On top of that, they have to keep track of balances and compare reports.

    Together, these tools power decisions about budgets and traffic. But every handoff takes time, and some data inevitably gets lost along the way.

    In a recent development, agencies feel it, too. At POSSIBLE earlier this year, the conversation turned to whether AI can finally break down those silos and perhaps eliminate a few steps along the way.

    In a recent development, the most important handoff in any AI workflow is the one from data to decision. AI can generate advertising copy and visuals very quickly at scale. But it can also optimize areas outside of the creative process: identifying outliers, explaining why a campaign behaves as it does, suggesting improvements, matching traffic with the right offers and taking over repetitive tasks.

    What we don’t discuss enough, however, is that AI is only as good as the data it works with. If the data is flawed or weak, all AI can do is help you make the wrong decision faster. Before automating decisions, it’s worth making sure you can trust the data.

    Some of the riskiest handoffs are the ones we don’t control at all, especially our dependence on platforms that can change the rules overnight.

    Industry observers note that in February, Google removed parked domains from its Search Partner Network, and a long-established monetization model suddenly became much harder to rely on. Last year, Chrome started automatically revoking notification permissions from sites if users ignore them. And, notably, Google’s decision to retire key Privacy Sandbox APIs highlighted how uncertain it is to wait for one significant replacement.

    It has been revealed that changes like these will keep coming. However, there is something we can do: Build businesses that adapt rapidly. When the parked-domain change happened, RollerAds didn’t start from scratch; we adapted the traffic monetization infrastructure we already had to work with domain traffic. In my experience, that’s what most real innovation looks like: spotting a shift early and building on what you already do well.

    The last handoff is between partners, and it only works if both sides trust what they’re seeing.

    It has been revealed that advertisers need to trust their partner platform and the traffic this platform provides. Publishers need to be able to predict their earnings. Affiliates need their conversions reported accurately. A great interface makes all of this easier to see, but what earns trust is what’s underneath: reliable tracking, fraud protection and clear, honest communication.

    If I could ask the industry for one thing, it would be to make ad tech understandable.

    At its core, the idea of digital advertising is simple: Show people relevant ads. But, over time, it has grown into a complex mix of acronyms, integrations and dashboards.

    It has been revealed that here’s my invitation to every platform: Before shipping the next feature, count the handoffs it removes. That’s the thinking behind RollerAds as a full-cycle ad platform. We’ve brought buying traffic, monetizing sites and running offers together in one account, and we keep looking for more steps to remove. The next big thing in ad tech may not be a thing at all. It will be the stage when tools combine into one seamless process with fewer handoffs, data we can trust, businesses that can absorb change and partners who make hard things simpler.

    We can start building it today.

    #20608. Which social platforms do Americans use to communicate? Depends who you ask.

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (421 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Which social platforms do Americans use to communicate? Depends who you ask.

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Pew Research Center has delivered its annual report on U.S.
    • According to recent reports, in last year’s Pew report, the top-ranked finishers were the platforms that best reached older Americans, and in 2026, that trend has essentially held true.
    • The platforms on the rise include some apps focused on communication.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Pew Research Center has delivered its annual report on U.S. social media usage, and as per usual, there are some revealing trends lurking within the demographic data. YouTube is still the most ubiquitous social platform among Americans, but beyond the top spot, the rankings differ depending on factors like age, gender, household income, and political orientation.

    According to recent reports, in last year’s Pew report, the top-ranked finishers were the platforms that best reached older Americans, and in 2026, that trend has essentially held true. YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram went 1-2-3 in the overall ranking and were the most-used social hubs in the 65-and-older age bracket.

    The platforms on the rise include some apps focused on communication. Adoption of both Snapchat and WhatsApp rose 1% year-over-year, but those companies are making gains within different communities. Snapchat’s user base still skews toward female users — it reaches 30% of U.S. women and 21% of U.S. men — while WhatsApp now reaches a higher percentage of U.S. men, which wasn’t the case a year ago.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that stats related to household income are also noteworthy. Snapchat is more common in U.S. households that make less than $70,000 per year, while WhatsApp reaches its highest percentage of Americans (40%) in households that eaern at least $100,000 per year.

    In general, social media use seems to be stratifying. Platforms like Facebook and TikTok tend to be more common in lower-income households. LinkedIn, as you would expect, appeals to Americans who are more well-off.

    Industry observers note that the economic polarization of U.S. social media can best be seen by examining the adoption of Nextdoor, which is a relatively new addition to Pew’s annual reports. The proportion of Americans using Nextdoor has risen by 5% over the past five years, but the community-oriented app is growing in particular communities. Only 9% of Americans in households making $30,000 or less per year use Nextdoor; in households where annual income exceeds $100,000, that percentage jumps to 23%.

    Are there any clear takeaways from these economic conditions? Perhaps some marketers will want to adjust platform spend to meet target consumers where they spend the most time. But the Pew rankings also show us that U.S. social media is inherently mutable. Beyond YouTube’s hold on the top spot, there’s plenty of room for change in each year’s rankings.

    • This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.
    • In a recent development, run risk assessments across the firm and major product changes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’re looking for a GRC Analyst to join our Compliance & Security team and help make risk management, audit and compliance a continuous part of how Supabase runs. You’ll work closely with engineering, security, IT, and legal to help us define our risk tolerance, keep our compliance programs (including SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022) current, test controls on a rolling basis, and answer customer and vendor security reviews quickly and accurately.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    In a recent development, run risk assessments across the firm and major product changes. Score likelihood and impact, propose treatments, and bring the results to leadership to inform risk tolerance decisions.

    Maintain the risk register, track remediation to closure, and report status to compliance and security leadership.

    According to recent reports, monitor controls on a rolling basis, using automated tests where they exist and manual testing where they don’t. Triage failures, prioritize by the risk register, and align each finding with an owner and a due date.

    Support internal audit, whether performed by an external partner or in-house: propose scope from the risk register, supply evidence, and track findings to closure.

    Run day-to-day operations for our compliance programs: evidence collection, control owner follow-up, and readiness ahead of each audit period.

    Extend continuous control validation beyond what our compliance platform covers. Build custom tests with AI coding tools, work with engineering and IT to pull evidence from source systems instead of collecting screenshots, and check that each test proves what the control requires.

    Have 3+ years of experience in GRC, internal audit, or security compliance at a SaaS or technology organization.

    Are comfortable working with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 controls, a compliance platform such as Drata, Vanta, and evidence from systems like AWS, GCP, Google Workspace, and Okta.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Have experience in async or globally distributed teams.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    Once a year, the entire firm gathers in a upcoming city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to our rundown of the most-watched branded YouTube videos of the week.
    • Recent findings suggest that we’re publishing this snippet of a larger Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report in order to analyze sponsorship trends in the creator economy.
    • Industry observers note that and–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to our rundown of the most-watched branded YouTube videos of the week.

    Recent findings suggest that we’re publishing this snippet of a larger Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report in order to analyze sponsorship trends in the creator economy. Any video released in tandem with an official brand partner is eligible for t he ranking.

    Industry observers note that and–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats. If you’re interested in learning more about Gospel–and which brands are sponsoring what creators on YouTube–click here. You can also download our YouTube 2025 Sponsorship Landscape Report here.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Boxing, golf, and football reign supreme in this week’s Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report, with sponsorships from DAZN, DraftKings, Lowe’s, and more.

    It has been revealed that #1 The Boy Who Punched Back ?? Channel: Zack D. Films Brand: DAZN Views: 13,632,976.

    Zack D. Films‘ DAZN promo starts like a Dhar Mann video: A kid, relentlessly bullied, finally has enough and stands up to his schoolyard oppressors.

    The Short keeps this inspirational tone, but it swings toward sports. Viewers learn the “kid” is actually world champion boxer Canelo Álvarez, and that after spending years at the top of his sport, he was defeated. Now, at 36, he wants to reclaim one of his old titles–World Boxing Council super middleweight champion–and to clinch it, he has to go up against undefeated young gun Christian Mbilli.

    And, of course, that match can only be watched on DAZN. The sports-specific streamer has been in our space since the Logan Paul vs KSI days, and continues to partner with creators for special events.

    #2 64 Golfers Compete For 4 Million Dollars | Internet Invitational Episode 1 Channel: Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, Barstool Sports, Internet Invitational Brand: Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, ZYRTEC Views: 12,095,382.

    And video #1 isn’t the only sports championship in the cards this week.

    Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, and Barstool Sports brought 64 creator golfers together for the Internet Invitational, which will pit them against each other on the green until just one puts their way to victory.

    According to recent reports, episode 1 of this tournament is over five hours long–which is a lot of airtime for sponsors Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, and ZYRTEC. We’re obviously intrigued by the tourney’s player lineup (which includes Dude Perfect‘s Tyler Toney, former Good Good-er Grant Horvat, TikToker Josh Richards, and Nelk Boys member Salim, with Barstool’s Dave Portnoy and pro golfer Kevin Kisner as rules officials), but we’re also intrigued by the brand choices. There’s some hefty companies here.

    It has been revealed that draftKings is basically a ubiquitous presence these days no matter which sport you’re watching–or which YouTube video. It paid for more than 80 videos this week alone. Then there’s Zyrtec, which we supposes connects here because these golfers are getting snootfuls of grass out on the green. (This is the only video Zyrtec sponsored.) Dunkin and Reese’s round out the snacks-and-drinks set, and prove once again that major food n bev brands are firmly committed to spending their marketing budgets in our space.

    #3 Making the worlds most extreme candy (it short-circuits my brain) Channel: NileBlue Brand: Brilliant Views: 12,475,822.

    He’s one of our few non-sports entrants this week, but NileBlue is still getting into the ring–and putting his tongue on the line.

    Sources indicate that his thesis is simple: candies like Warheads are trying to give the eater a truly unpleasant experience. But none of them are quite overwhelming enough.

    It has been revealed that “I think this is mostly because they’re all trying to only assault one thing at a time,” Nile states. “Which personallly, I think is a mistake, because it leaves so many completely available tastebuds completely unaffected. And what I really want is a candy that targets everything.”.

    That means a candy which is sour, sweet, spicy, icy, bitter, salty, and umami to the max, all at the same time.

    Can he succeed? Viewers who lock in for his full 38-minute journey will be rewarded with the answer (and sponsor Brilliant will be rewarded with their watch time).

    Sources indicate that #4 LIVE with Lowes playing Madden 27, featuring Justin Jefferson! #ad Channel: MMG Brand: Lowe’s Views: 11,333,221.

    Our final sports video of the week is from OG Madden YouTuber MMG, who’s joined by Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson for a chat and a few rounds in Madden 27.

    Industry observers note that the YouTube world and the sports world are becoming increasingly intertwined (just look at the above creator invitational, for example), so it’s not as unusual to see athletes popping up on creators’ channels, but it’s still cool every time. MMG launched his channel in 2015, and after 11 years of work, he’s sitting pretty with NFL stars.

    This stream was part of the Lowe’s “Earn Your Sunday” campaign, which urges dudes to get their sh*t done around the house so they can kick back and watch the weekend games. As part of the deal, MMG gave away a signed Jefferson helmet and jersey; viewers who head over to the Lowe’s website will also see another, bigger giveaway for the “ultimate Super Bowl Sunday.” Lowe’s is definitely putting stock into making the end of this NFL season a touchdown.

    BONUS #2,410 I Played Skyrim as a Lore Accurate Vampire Channel: OSK Gaming Brand: Idle Obelisk Miner Views: 124,561.

    In honor of everyone who waited 15 years for a name reveal, we brought in OSK Gaming and his very dedicated Skyrim playthrough as our bonus video.

    Bethesda Game Studios boss Todd Howard has a contentious reputation among gamers, and OSK has another gripe for the pile: He’s pretty sure the ol’ Todd hates vampires. So what’s a guy to do if he wants to play a real vampire within the sprawling fantasy world of Skyrim? You download a boatload of mods and do it yourself. Who cares if Skyrim won’t let you be a real vampire? OSK is gonna make it happen anyway.

    On his journey, he’ll actually be playing two games, thanks to his sponsor Idle Obelisk Miner. As you may expect from the name, IOM is an idle title, where you get set up and then all you have to do is check in on things every once in a while. What you might not expect is that one game title would sponsor a video about another completely unrelated game. But this is the perfect pairing. While OSK hikes across Skyrim, IOM runs in the background, so he can game while he games.

    …and there’s a lot more data where that came from. If you like our Weekly Top 5, you’ll love everything else Gospel has to offer.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer to join our Turso core database team and help bring forward the future of agentic databases. Turso is both an Open Source database that replaces SQLite—with an ongoing project to also support the Postgres interface—and a Cloud offering where customers can create databases on demand. You’ll work closely with customers and other teams at Supabase to build the future of what databases look like in a world where users and agents are creating millions of databases a day.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building database technology tools that scale to billions.

    Driving the progress of the Turso Open Source database, in particular the Postgres compatibility layer.

    Making sure code works, and never breaks, and putting the systems and guarantees in place for that to happen.

    Maintaining the Turso Cloud operations, including the Cloud API and data plane operations.

    Improving the scalability of the Turso Cloud operations to support a 100x larger number of databases.

    Have written databases before, and/or other high-stakes low-level systems like Hypervisors, OS Kernels, storage devices, etc.

    Have experience working with remote teams and Open Source communities.

    Have a passion and experience for correct systems that work, and have the experience in the tools to make that happen: Deterministic Simulation Testing, formal verification methods, fuzz and differential testing, etc.

    Have experience deploying, operating and debugging large scale software systems in production in cloud environments such as AWS & Kubernetes.

    Have experience improving the observability, reliability and performance of complex cloud systems.

    Are comfortable working in Rust.

    Are comfortable with LLM-assisted development and evals.

    Are comfortable working with Embedded databases.

    Communicate clearly across both technical and non-technical audiences.

    Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving rapidly.

    Recent findings suggest that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    In a recent development, every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.
