    It has been revealed that in the next two years, we aim to help over 250,000 Americans get access to life-changing benefits. Behind that impact is a remarkable group of people — attorneys, engineers, client advocates, marketers, product managers, and more. The Atticus People team makes that work possible — we build the systems, policies and operations that enable us to do our best work.

    In a recent development, we’re hiring a People Operations Lead to run the backbone of our People function: benefits, systems, payroll and multi-state compliance through our PEO, people policy, and our performance and merit cycles. You’ll be the day-to-day owner of how this work gets done — managing our vendors, keeping us compliant as we grow, running our cycles cleanly, and improving the employee experience at every touchpoint. You’ll also play a central role in the bigger decisions ahead of us — when and how we leave our PEO, how we replace our HRIS, how our policies and benefits should evolve — bringing the analysis and recommendations that shape them.

    In a recent development, you’ll report to Amy Yu, our Head of People, and join a small, high-ownership team that cares deeply about our mission and about having real impact. The ideal candidate has run core People Operations programs at a tech-driven company and is ready to take on a broader scope somewhere the work really matters. We’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people get the benefits they deserve, and the people doing that work are who you’d be building for.

    5+ years in People Operations at a venture-backed tech company, with hands-on ownership of at least a few of: benefits, HRIS, payroll, compliance, performance cycles, and policies.

    You’re equally comfortable running a benefits analysis as you are having a tough leave conversation, and handle both with tact and clarity.

    You’ve administered an HRIS end-to-end and managed People vendors and partners; you’ve driven a system implementation or migration and know what makes one go well.

    You’ve automated and improved HR processes to be more efficient, accurate and seamless for both HR and business users.

    You operate with low ego but high ownership, and are comfortable both doing the work and figuring out how it can be improved.

    In a recent development, the role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup that doubles as a B-corp social enterprise. Our team is still small enough for you to have an outsized impact on how we operate and how our people experience unfolds.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employee and family premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    Sources indicate that we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $120,000 to $160,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate’s experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the tech giant dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    • The upcoming counts, it remarked, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it remarked its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.

    The upcoming counts, it remarked, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”.

    Sources indicate that but the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation. Data from Agentio highlighted public viewcounts over-reported actual views by 40%; experiments by individual creators like John Green, who compared his backend viewcount of one video to its public-facing count, found similar inaccuracy.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Now, the Interactive Advertising Bureau has released a report, The Creator Economy’s Next Chapter, that calls for wide standardization of what counts as a “view.”.

    Accurate measurement is the “fault line beneath the creator economy,” the IAB said in its report. This overall conclusion came from 53 participating industry leaders who filled out the IAB’s survey, and also from senior industry leader interviews conducted by the IAB’s Creator Economy Board.

    It has been revealed that “Measurement also sits inside problems that look like something else. Two sides who disagree on creator pricing both agree they cannot judge whether creators are paid fairly because nobody agrees what creator content is worth,” the IAB wrote. “One in eight respondents traced budget fights with leadership to measurement gaps, and a similar share stated organizations withhold results because the numbers behind them are not solid enough to publish.”.

    We see why this is a major concern: Brands pay creators based on their reach, so when platforms like YouTube roll out changes that inflate views, marketers end up overpaying.

    According to recent reports, it might not sound bad for creators to make a little extra cash, but this situation doesn’t end well for them either. If they secure a brand deal based on inflated views, that sets a high bar for engagement that their sponsored content almost certainly will not clear. This performance gap might result in them losing their relationship with that individual brand, or with an entire agency that represents other crucial brands in their niche.

    It’s not just marketers that told the IAB standardization is needed. “Measurement providers, who see the problem most closely, were unanimous in choosing a common definition of a view as a top priority,” the bureau remarked in its report.

    Recent findings suggest that they also have a proposed solution: “Respondents are clear about where to start. Given 11 possible standards, two-thirds (66%) chose a common definition of a view and exposure metrics across platforms,” per the report. “Each platform counts a view differently, and shared reporting format, cross-channel planning, and any comparison with video or television all depend on counting it the same way.”.

    It has been revealed that among the IAB’s respondents, another interesting data point emerged. The majority of entities that produce metrics (like platforms, marketing agencies, and measurement companies) say they are “very confident” in the accuracy of the numbers they provide.

    Meanwhile brands and talent agencies both said they have zero percent confidence in numbers they receive.

    The IAB claims to rectify this problem, it plans to work alongside the Media Ratings Council and other “engaged industry bodies” to bring content platforms and measurement providers together so everyone can agree on cross-platform definitions of a view, an impression, reach, and watch time.

    It says it hopes to secure one to two platform agreements within the first year of this effort.

    If it does that, we might be looking at one of the biggest industry shifts to date, and could end up in a radically different era of social media and content creation.

    35% of respondents said creators’ work split across teams and tools is not working. 33% said brands don’t understand creators’ channels. 31% cited pricing inconsistency, and 25% said agreeing on contract and deal terms is difficult.

    Solutions they suggested include standard T&Cs and contracts for creator x bran deals (66% of respondents), transparency standards for agency fee disclosure (38%), and a unified creator taxonomy (31%).

    You can read the IAB’s full report here.

    Sources indicate that invest in customer connections to build a trust-based relationship. Everyday CSA’s work with the production data stores of startups and enterprises alike. Building trust in the Success team and Supabase platform is paramount to a successful customer relationship.

    Sources indicate that as TwitchCon descends upon San Diego, a different hub for video game streaming is celebrating its ascendance. TikTok Live is the fastest growing platform in that category, according to a fresh report published by the GameSquare subsidiary Hatchet.

    Hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual enhancement related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.

    Sources indicate that previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals. While TikTok Live watch time grew 96% year-over-year, Twitch and YouTube Gaming’s respective market shares both went down.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, through properties like Hatchet, FaZe Clan, and TubeBuddy, GameSquare has made deep inroads in digital gaming communities. “Hatchet’s latest report highlights just how quickly TikTok Live has established itself in gaming live-streaming,” stated GameSquare CEO Justin Kenna in a statement. “Nearly doubling its gaming hours watched in a year is a clear signal that audience habits are shifting toward mobile, discovery-driven viewing.”.

    It has been revealed that kenna cited titles like Roblox, Garena Free Fire, and Mobile Legends as three major drivers of TikTok Live’s watch time uptick. Roblox led all games in terms of TikTok Live watch time during the first half of 2026; it generated 631 million hours of TikTok viewership during that period.

    In a recent development, roblox is a favorite of Gen Alpha gamers, while Free Fire and Mobile Legends appeal to gamers on mobile devices, especially outside of the United States. Those two data points help explain how TikTok Live has managed such a sizable gaming glow-up — it has volume none of its competitors can match. With 1.4 million creators active each day, TikTok Live’s community is nearly twice as significant as Twitch’s.

    According to recent reports, that massive quantity has made TikTok Live a market leader across multiple streaming categories. Its gaming operation, however, is one of its strongest fortes, and rival platforms should be prepared to see more growth from their ByteDance-owned competitor.

    The $4 million Internet Invitational might become golf’s next big thing — or another bogey

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all.
    • The driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports.
    • It has been revealed that the first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all. I’m talking about the Internet Invitational, which recently wrapped up its second season by splitting a $4 million prize among the 16 members of the winning team.

    The driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports. To create an event that could demonstrate the influence and appeal of the “YouTube golf” scene, Portnoy teamed up with Robby Berger and his Bob Does Sports brand.

    It has been revealed that the first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize. The event was put on as a response to the PGA’s uneven investment in golf personalities. The Creator Classic that had signaled the PGA’s interest in digital partnerships was not held at TPC Sawgrass in 2026.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    It has been revealed that portnoy and Berger bet that they could outdo the PGA by fully embracing golf creators, and they doubled down in 2026, when they quadrupled the size of the Internet Invitational prize. “It’s all because of Dave, man,” Barstool Sports video editor Brendan Jones told Golf magazine. “Dave puts up all this money, and that changes people. That’s not good or bad — it just changes the way that people act, right? Dave’s massive thing with anything that we do at Barstool, it’s like, what are the stakes? Why do people care? How are we going to get anything out of them?”.

    In a recent development, in this case, people care because the proceedings were sillier, wackier, and more relatable than anything a PGA-sanctioned event could deliver. There were breakout stars like Paige Spiranac, wildly varied handicaps, and plenty of substance use during the tournament. And the fans loved it. Viewership hit 3.5 million during the first 24 hours and ballooned past 11 million views within a week.

    “When you put the average Joe, who’s not a great golfer— that, to I think a lot of people, was riveting,” Berger told The Hollywood Reporter. “I mean, it’s kind of what Bob Does Sports was built off of.”.

    Sources indicate that as exciting as the action may have been, the Internet Invitational wasn’t free from drama. Nelk member Salim Sirur‘s excessive drinking and Sam Heung Min‘s criticisms related to rules enforcement added controversy to the event’s conclusion. Given Portnoy’s controversial past and the indiscretions of some substantial names in the YouTube golf community (looking at you, Good Good), one wonders how long the Internet Invitational can sustain its positive momentum.

    But the success of the tournament’s second iteration can’t be ignored. With the decline of LIV Golf and the presence of elite golfers on YouTube, there’s an opportunity for creators to build a viable alternative to the PGA Tour. To do that will take continued dedication from the people who made the Internet Invitational happen — and the golfers might want to cut down on the drinking, too.

    We sit on one of the largest labeled corpora of live web-server malware in the industry: files, verdicts, cleanup outcomes, and analyst decisions collected from production hosting servers every day. It already drives our signatures, heuristics, and ML models, and there is far more to get out of it. We are looking for a Senior ML Engineer who will turn that data into detection that ships — classifiers, LLM-assisted triage and generated signatures — and keep exploring fresh ML/LLM methods against it, measured by the product's false-negative and false-positive rates, not by notebook accuracy.

    Our dataset focuses on web malware — PHP, JavaScript, HTML phishing kits, infected WordPress and Joomla plugins and themes, database injections — with the context around each file.

    Sources indicate that the goal is 10x more malware detected at the same or lower false-positive rate. Hand-written rules and faster pipelines will not get there; models trained on our data might.

    You get an experimentation track, GPUs, and a direct line to leadership; in return, you bring numbers, not opinions.

    You own the path from raw samples to a model in production, and the numbers that prove it helped.

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.
    • Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.
    • “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform said in a tech giant post.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.

    Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.

    “Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform said in a tech giant post. “Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so new viewers can find your work and keep watching. Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X. The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards. Everyone wins when great moments travel.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, as you very likely know, clipping is the method du jour for creators to spread the word about their stuff. Sometimes fans clip for free/for the love of the game, but in many cases, creators pay people to clip their long-form videos and spread the shorter vids across platforms, hoping to drive more people to their full-length YouTube videos, Twitch streams, or podcast episodes.

    It has been revealed that with its clipping tool–which, from the announcement video, looks like a basic trimmer with no real editing capabilities–X is telling creators, Hey, you don’t have to worry about hiring clippers for our platform. We’ll do it. That could be an upside for creators who don’t want to compensate people themselves.

    Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X.

    Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so newly introduced viewers can find your work and keep watching.

    Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X.

    According to recent reports, the best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards.

    Everyone wins when great moments travel. Clipping is one more step toward making X the best place to create, grow and earn.

    — Creators (@XCreators) November 9, 2026.

    According to recent reports, X, however, is offering a blanket green light. We’re not sure Elon Musk‘s platform will pay enough to tempt pro clippers, but it might appeal to aspiring clippers who seek a lower barrier to entry.

    It has been revealed that to be clear, though, we don’t know how much X will pay clippers. It claims they’ll earn money through its rewards program, which pays a set amount based on engagement metrics, but how will revenue be split between creator and clipper?

    Recent findings suggest that also worth noting: Not everyone can join the rewards program. X has to approve you first.

    Recent findings suggest that like we mentioned above, this is far from X’s first attempt to woo creators. Not long after Musk bought it, X (still called Twitter at that point…RIP) increased its max video length to 60 minutes, clearly hoping to pull some YouTubers. Musk himself personally appealed to MrBeast, who obliged and put a long-form video on X in early 2024; he did not seem overly impressed by the results, and has stayed firmly on YouTube, where he’s the biggest fish around.

    Other tweaks X has made include abolishing Twitter’s iconic character limit (thus attempting to challenge YouTube text posts as well as newsletter hubs like Substack), letting creators paywall posts, and adding a “completely redesigned livestreaming control room.” That last launch came with a promise to shell out a total of $1 million to streamers who went live on X.

    • Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

    This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

    Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly said in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

    WhatCultureGaming introduces newly introduced YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The proposal is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

    Anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

    Recent findings suggest that elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

    In a recent development, meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

    Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a fresh dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

    In a recent development, hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have massive shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

    Recent findings suggest that the first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the new ceremony.

    Kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a new type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

    Industry observers note that GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game introduces, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

    Barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

    In a recent development, celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

    In a recent development, shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a upcoming gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

    Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets customers decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on big purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

    Hearst is working with creators to execute original content and brand deals on the fly

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (436 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that hearst Communications has a long history of working alongside influencers, and it is bringing that effort into the current phase of the creator economy.
    • It has been revealed that according to Adweek, Hearst’s new venture will be active across five of its editorial brands, including Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend.
    • Recent findings suggest that though Hearst is nearly 140 years old, it has never been shy about incorporating digital creators into its editorial brands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that hearst Communications has a long history of working alongside influencers, and it is bringing that effort into the current phase of the creator economy. A fresh venture called Hearst Creator Studios combines elements of a talent agency with the structure of a creator network to establish a unit that can deliver original content and branded media.

    It has been revealed that according to Adweek, Hearst’s new venture will be active across five of its editorial brands, including Cosmopolitan, Elle, and MotorTrend. More than 50 creators are involved, and Hearst is splitting them into two groups. So-called “creators at large” will be contracted to produce content, including at least seven original series. The rest of the creators will be “friends of the brand” who will be plugged into an internal, searchable platform that can be accessed by producers and brands.

    Recent findings suggest that though Hearst is nearly 140 years old, it has never been shy about incorporating digital creators into its editorial brands. Its attempts to turn on that pipeline have evolved alongside the creator economy. A decade ago, Hearst invested in multi-channel networks to gain access to the creator lineups assembled therein. In 2020, its U.K. arm established an “influence network” meant to increase its social media presence. Other Hearst experiments have involved original programming, TikTok integrations, and Reddit-esque upvotes.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recently, brands have discovered an exciting latest way to harness social media influence: Creator programs. That’s the name given to in-house networks that turn popular creators into brand spokespeople. After companies like Home Depot pioneered the concept, brands like Nat Geo have applied it to the realm of editorial content.

    That being said, Hearst Magazines EVP and Global Chief Revenue Officer Lisa Ryan Howard told Adweek that the company’s Creator Studios is not a creator program. Instead, editors-in-chief handpick creator partners and appoint talent managers to work alongside those creators’ reps.

    It has been revealed that the result is a venture that operates most similarly to a talent agency. “Marketers want this because they want a curatorial eye on the creators,” Howard stated, “as well as a one-stop shop.”.

    Sources indicate that the early output from Hearst Creator Studios includes The Feelings Department, which comes from creators Izzy Perez and Emma Fuente and hits Cosmopolitan accounts in November. The plan is to increase the program’s output in 2027, when the 30-plus brands in Hearst’s editorial portfolio will gain access to a burgeoning network of creator partners.

    Elsewhere in the ranking, a one-time collaborator of MrBeast’s is making waves on his own. One of Latin America’s biggest creators has taken advantage of spooky season while tying in a cultural phenomenon that has had a consistent presence within our charts.

    Recent findings suggest that mrBeast isn’t involved in Vigevani’s biggest video of 2026, but a creepy clown is. After claiming to purchase the clown on the dark web, Vigevani used it as the primary prop in a multi-part series that drew inspiration from the smash-hit, YouTube-born franchise Backrooms.

    Vigevani dropped his Backrooms-inspired series in the middle of spooky season, and that approach paid off. The ninth installment of the series, which arrived on November 11, was particular popular. It already has nearly 40 million views, and Vigevani has called it his biggest video of the year.

    The culmination of Vigevani’s clown serial pushed him up to 27th place in the Global Top 50. He collected 413.1 million weekly views, increasing his YouTube traffic by 28% week-over-week in the process.

    Recent findings suggest that english-speaking consumers might think that clown horror is so ten years ago. Back in 2016, a viral clown craze turned into a veritable panic in the days surrounding Halloween. That experience convinced many that clowns are too creepy to belong at children’s parties.

    In Latin America, however, clown content still has legs. One of the biggest channels in the region is El Payaso Plim Plim, a clown who isn’t afraid to remain kid-friendly. We’ve had regular Plim Plim sightings in our charts for years, and that trend has continued into 2026. There hasn’t been a week over the past six months in which Plim Plim has collected fewer than 250 million views.

    Vigevani has found a clever way to apply that interest in clowns to a more adult audience. By leaning into the inherent horror of pale faces and colorful makeup, Vigevani has revived a decade-old craze and picked up tens of millions of views in the process.

    I doubt Plim Plim, who appeals to young children, would approve of Vigevani’s recharacterization of clowns. But that’s what happens when you get your clown on the dark web — you don’t always get what you pay for.

    Industry News: Substack management firm Brigade snapped up by Hollywood’s Entertainment 360

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Entertainment 360, the Hollywood talent and literary management manufacturer that reps celebrities like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore, has acquired Brigade, a digital talent firm that specializes in Substack writers and podcasters.
    • As part of the deal, Brigade founder Max Stein will join Entertainment 360 as a Partner.
    • Among those clients are notable Substack writers Leandra Medine Cohen (a well-known fashion maven) and Emily Sundberg, who writes daily business newsletter Feed Me, as well as podcast host/creative consultant Chris Black and celebrity stylist Danielle Goldberg.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Entertainment 360, the Hollywood talent and literary management manufacturer that reps celebrities like Margot Robbie and Julianne Moore, has acquired Brigade, a digital talent firm that specializes in Substack writers and podcasters.

    As part of the deal, Brigade founder Max Stein will join Entertainment 360 as a Partner. He’ll bring with him Brigade’s team of managers and the firm’s ~40 clients, all of whom will keep their current representatives, he told The Upcoming York Times.

    Among those clients are notable Substack writers Leandra Medine Cohen (a well-known fashion maven) and Emily Sundberg, who writes daily business newsletter Feed Me, as well as podcast host/creative consultant Chris Black and celebrity stylist Danielle Goldberg.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that hollywood’s interest in creators has been the major buzz for a while, but that interest tends to zero in on moviemakers. Brigade’s clients–particularly its Substack contingent–are from other, oft-overlooked disciplines where digital talent and legacy entertainment could mesh.

    “I’ve always been drawn to people with a singular point of view, whose work and ambitions don’t fit neatly into one category,” Stein, who got his start in fashion and debuted Brigade in 2015, said in a statement. “Our clients have built remarkable careers by following their own taste and instincts, and our job has been to help them turn those ideas into lasting businesses.”.

    Entertainment 360 Partner Darin Friedman told The Hollywood Reporter that the worlds of digital and legacy entertainment “have collapsed a bit on each other.”.

    “YouTube is competing with Netflix, and Netflix is buying podcasts, and Disney is wanting to set meetings with comedians who want to develop TV shows,” he added.

    In a separate statement, Entertainment 360’s Partners collectively said they’ve noticed “[t]he ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today.”.

    “Bringing Brigade into 360 expands what we can offer our clients and strengthens our ability to create extraordinary opportunities for artists across an increasingly diverse entertainment landscape,” they added.

    Stein, meanwhile, told NYT that Brigade’s digital clients “are still attracted to some of the more legacy things.”.

    Sundberg took to LinkedIn to offer her own perspective on the deal.

    “I’d be nervous if I were one of two groups of people–teams at the giant talent agencies like WME and United Talent Agency who aren’t spending time learning about the economics and opportunities of platforms like Substack; and Substack’s internal ad team, who needs to learn how to work with agencies like Entertainment 360 (and Spur and Amplifier and Alltogether) who already have deep relationships with advertisers,” she said.

    Substack might be one step ahead there: As Digiday spotted today, Substack has a latest job listing out for a U.S.-based Product Manager of Payments. The role’s description states the manager will handle gifting, retention offers, and improvement to payment and subscription experiences, along with advertising monetization–all with the (presumed) goal of getting creators paid more.

    Industry observers note that substack already pumped up newsletter sponsorships earlier this year, debuting Creator Kits to help writers secure brand deals. Other creator-friendly adds to its service include a TikTok-style promo feed and a $20 million Creator Accelerator Fund.

    360 and Brigade didn’t disclose financials of their acquisition, but we’re betting they both see potential gold in uniting across largely unexplored territory.

    Scope and run proofs-of-concept against clear, shared success criteria, guiding customers all the way to production.

    Reason with customers about connectivity, infrastructure, and end-to-end latency to design for scale and reliability.

    Create technical content — blog posts, guides, webinars, and conference talks — that helps developers and enterprises build with LiveKit.

    Act as the technical enabler for your region's pod, and share field insight with Product and Engineering to help shape the roadmap.

    Breaking: Top Million Sites Lost 12% Of Visits; Top 100’s Share Barely Moved via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro.
    • Rand Fishkin, SparkToro’s co-founder and CEO, wrote that the project began with his theory that the biggest sites, largely Substantial Tech properties, were taking more of the web’s traffic.
    • In a recent development, the post also reports a 29.2% drop in visits per internet user.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro. The proportion of visits that go to websites that are not among the top 100 stayed relatively consistent over this time. That means while the total number of visits was down, that proportion still added up to less traffic for non-top-100 sites.

    Rand Fishkin, SparkToro’s co-founder and CEO, wrote that the project began with his theory that the biggest sites, largely Substantial Tech properties, were taking more of the web’s traffic.

    In a recent development, the post also reports a 29.2% drop in visits per internet user. This calculation uses user estimates that were revised partway through the period.

    Fishkin asked Similarweb for total visits to the top million sites from its worldwide desktop and mobile web panel, along with a breakdown by site rank.

    In a recent development, in the post’s figures, total visits peaked in Q1 2022 at 2.243 trillion. At the low point in Q1 2026, the total was 1.914 trillion, down 14.7% from the peak. The latest quarter, Q3 2026, came in at 1.970 trillion, 12.2% below the peak.

    The totals on the post’s chart stay roughly level through 2023, then dip in early 2024 and fall again in the first half of 2025.

    Similarweb categorized the top million websites from the number 1-10 to the 100,001st to 1 millionth website by five levels of ranking.

    The share chart shows roughly a combined 33% and 36% of visits for the #1-10 (top) and #11-100 (next 90) sites during Q4 2021 and Q3 2026 respectively. The percentages for each band below the top 100 were a little lower at the end of the period compared to the beginning.

    Fishkin described growth in the share for the top 100 as small, writing that “stagnation is a more accurate description of the trend.”.

    SparkToro’s per-user number is found by dividing Similarweb’s total visits by DataReportal’s estimated quarterly internet consumers globally. The table included in the blog post reports 4.95 billion internet users in Q4 2021 and 6.15 billion for Q3 2026. This represents an increase of around 24% during that time. The blog post reports the decline in visits per user at 29.2%.

    Recent findings suggest that the user series jumped from 5.65 billion to 6.04 billion in one quarter (Q3) of 2025. According to DataReportal in their October 2025 report, this jump in the number of customers online was “largely attributable to significant revisions” in the rate of internet use that were officially reported by India and China. They also warned the reader to avoid interpreting this change as if hundreds of millions of new people came online in 90 days.

    The SparkToro post did not include information regarding the change in reporting. Their estimate of 24% user growth compared data prior to and subsequent to the reporting change.

    Similarweb’s panel tracks browser visits on desktop and mobile, but not app use. Fishkin wrote that consolidation by Big Tech is likely much more common in apps.

    According to recent reports, the data is also worldwide, and he wrote that it’s plausible traffic to U.S., U.K. and EU sites declined while regions with growing internet access, such as Asia and Africa, grew. The post doesn’t break out regions or state the panel’s size.

    It has been revealed that he did not provide reasons for the decline in visits. Fishkin’s list of possible factors includes app-only use, reliance on search engine results, AI tool utilization, social media platforms and the user behavior changes after the COVID-19 pandemic.

    Recent findings suggest that after initial publication SparkToro updated their article. On Nov. 10, Fishkin noted on X that the prior version of his post “had an incorrect graph/data.” That version’s headline put the decline at 24%, which the URL still indicates.

    SparkToro sells audience research software, and Fishkin co-authored the book “Zero Click Marketing.”.

    Sources indicate that sparkToro has provided an international benchmark for when a multi-year traffic decline shows up in your reports. The percentage of visits based upon the ranking of the website held close to steady in Similarweb’s browser-based metrics, although the actual number of visits decreased. The headline statistic in the report without reliance on changes in user estimates is the 12.2 percent decline in overall visits.

    This report measures the number of browser visits to the top million websites regardless of where they came from, whereas the zero-click data I reported on back in June measured clicks per U.S. Google search.

    Sources indicate that until a regional breakdown is available, SparkToro’s figures are best viewed as global context for traffic conversations, rather than as a benchmark for any single market. Fishkin also wrote that he plans to compare the findings with other sources and revisit the numbers every year or two.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • Recent findings suggest that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of.
    • Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of newly introduced databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

    Recent findings suggest that container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

    Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

    The work spans three strength areas:.

    Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

    Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

    Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

    Industry observers note that we expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

    Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

    Platform reliability & operations.

    Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

    Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for new platform capabilities and major changes.

    Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

    Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

    Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

    Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

    Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

    Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

    Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

    Tooling, ecosystem & architecture.

    Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

    Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

    Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

    Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

    Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

    Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):.

    Tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

    Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

    Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

    In a recent development, have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

    Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

    Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

    Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

    Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

    Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

    Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

    Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire tech giant gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Recent findings suggest that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #20538. Does The Affiliate Model Survive Checkout Inside AI Mode And Gemini? – Ask An SEO via @sejournal, @rollerblader

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Does The Affiliate Model Survive Checkout Inside AI Mode And Gemini? – Ask An SEO via @sejournal, @rollerblader

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This week’s Ask an SEO is about affiliate marketing, which is actually one of my favorite topics to cover.
    • Recent findings suggest that “With Google’s UCP and checkout happening inside Gemini and AI Mode, the shopper never clicks my link.
    • Great question, and yes, affiliate links still matter, so make sure you keep using them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This week’s Ask an SEO is about affiliate marketing, which is actually one of my favorite topics to cover.

    Recent findings suggest that “With Google’s UCP and checkout happening inside Gemini and AI Mode, the shopper never clicks my link. Does the affiliate model survive this, and what should I be doing now?”.

    Great question, and yes, affiliate links still matter, so make sure you keep using them. It is similar to Shopify having the Google Direct Checkout UCP. That doesn’t mean you don’t need to keep your Shopify store, but you also want to make sure you are protected with multiple ways to monetize and that you work with brands that focus on more than just links.

    This is why there is a question. If the person doesn’t make it to the link, do links matter? Yes, and this goes back to the history of links.

    It has been revealed that the message displayed was a benefit to them, to let them know that if they logged in, they could add to their cart and check out later when they have more time vs. needing to do everything right now. When they logged in, we could sync up the sale with the original click, and the affiliate would get credit. This led to fingerprinting and many more advanced techniques the networks (like Buy.at at the time) began working on.

    There are also affiliate companies that show ads via streaming TV highlights and track the IPs connected to the same connection to track affiliate sales back. They count the IPs against consumer data sent back to the network and get credit for the sale.

    In a recent development, the reason I mention this is because, clicks don’t always matter, but they do add levels of tracking security for you. There is IP hashing, companies like TV Scientific and AudioHook are using alternative tracking methods, and vanity codes. Just make sure your vanity code doesn’t get leaked to coupon websites, browser extensions, and that AI doesn’t start showing them to traffic you didn’t refer.

    See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It.

    Industry observers note that being afraid of Google taking the order and cutting your link out is a valid concern. But think about TikTok Shop, or retailer apps inside ChatGPT like Walmart’s, which keep the purchase on the platform. These cut your link out completely. The person may read your content then go to TikTok for a review and purchase there.

    You have significant brands that allow third parties to sell on their website (i.e., marketplaces), and with some you don’t get commissions for those sales as they’re third party vendors. Your links matter and clicks tracked, but the conversion is not commissionable. In the case of systems like TikTok, use links on your website and upload content to their platform to make money with your vendors that are synced there. You control the situation, don’t stress over a single link on the website.

    Recent findings suggest that for programs that allow third-party sales and don’t pay, select other programs. That is a choice you are knowingly making and you are knowingly sending your traffic there.

    See also: Getting Your Product Into ChatGPT Isn’t The Hard Part, Getting It Through Checkout Is.

    Another reason to not stop using affiliate links is that consumers do not trust AI. Keynote speakers at college graduations keep getting booed when they talk about it; younger generations are avoiding brands that use it for creating images; people are starting to engage less with AI ads on social media and convert less when the content and images are clearly AI on a website (blog posts, product pages, etc.).

    Recent findings suggest that when AI is used, there’s no way to know if the store and ad are legit, or if they’re a third-party counterfeit produced overseas. Reviews are also being gamed. Consumers may not trust the AI Overview as much if quality doesn’t improve, and if they don’t like AI, they will instead scroll down to your content, where they can be exposed to your link.

    There is another layer to affiliate links mattering as well.

    AI Overviews cannot demonstrate a product or service. Yes, they can play a video, but Google search has done this for years. People, especially those who do not trust AI, will keep looking for human-created content before making the purchase. This is especially true for larger-ticket items like bikes, software, or computer systems, and demonstrations of video games before buying them. Think of parents who want to make sure it is age-appropriate, or someone who wants to see what the graphics and games are like from an actual gamer.

    This makes your affiliate links directly relevant, and in your advertising disclosure you can let them know that by clicking your link they are helping to support your business and not AI. This will resonate strongly with the anti-AI generations and shoppers. It is also required by the FTC and some international groups that you use advertising disclosures, so you might as well.

    See also: Only 28% Of Americans Trust AI Search – And That Gap Is Your SEO Opening.

    There is affordable technology from third parties like ThoughtMetrics (I have zero relationship with them, just a happy user) that indicates all touchpoints in a customer journey (and repeat purchases for LTV). If you didn’t use your affiliate link, you won’t be in the running for credit or a commission. In another program, we reconcile at the end of the month and manually add anything that didn’t track. If that click didn’t happen, you would not be making as much money.

    Recent findings suggest that link clicks are always going to be an issue, but they are also still working and a first line of defense in your ability to get credit for your referrals. So yes, affiliate links and clicks still matter; there are just additional layers of protection available with more advanced tracking techniques.

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the manufacturer’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30.

    In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.”.

    The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is at the moment no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

    Recent findings suggest that “News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey mentioned in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their customers), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.”.

    Industry observers note that NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey remarked, should focus on four core issues:.

    (i) the specific Meta Firm Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content;.

    (ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products;.

    (iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized;.

    (iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected.

    Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.”.

    Sources indicate that the World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its latest subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world.

    The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” remarked CMDG director Courtney Radsch. “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.”.

    On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.”.

    “The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” mentioned Tim Cowen, a MOW cofounder.

    In a recent development, MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter, who noted during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review.

    On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s upcoming terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.”.

    According to recent reports, “Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.”.

    It has been revealed that “Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.”.

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

    RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

    Industry observers note that nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”.

    The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

    “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

    A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the manufacturer revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”.

    In a recent development, as of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    “I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”.

    Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”.

    The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said.

    Sources indicate that “My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner mentioned. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its fresh terms.”.

    News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the firm suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

    Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the upcoming terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

    In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter mentioned he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

    According to recent reports, “The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important matter,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”.

    Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all users worldwide, starting today. Sites that track how often AI Mode cites them now have a upcoming model to account for.

    In an X thread announcing the change, Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, said Hydrogen is also “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google’s Search post says the model is available globally in Search for all users.

    Industry observers note that the switch came two days into the November core enhancement, which was still rolling out as of 2:05 p.m. ET today.

    The Search post says Hydrogen is able to handle multi-part inquiries, inquiries that contain typos, highly specific inquiries, and follow commands more thoroughly than previous versions of Search.

    According to recent reports, the post from Search says that Hydrogen also allows for better query fan-out. Query fan-out refers to how Search simultaneously executes multiple queries across each of the subtopics of an inquiry. According to the post, the result is what Google calls “connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before,” and this includes websites which users may have never stumbled upon themselves. Stein’s thread says that the fan-out improvements result in showing more links to the web. Neither the post nor Stein’s thread provide counts for links or sites.

    The post references more visual aids in answers through use of images, structured responses, comparison tables and additional customized tools available to users; additionally, the answers provided will be more nuanced in all languages supported by AI Mode.

    The last default change I covered was at I/O back in May when Gemini 3.5 Flash became the global default for AI Mode for everyone. Neither the Search post nor Stein’s post stated what Hydrogen replaced.

    Stein’s thread has Hydrogen handling the hardest AI Overview questions but doesn’t say which questions count as hardest or what answers the rest. The Search post doesn’t mention AI Overviews.

    Google made Gemini 3 the default model for AI Overviews globally in January. At the time, I noted that Google had described looks to send complex questions to Gemini 3 and simpler ones to faster models, and hadn’t mentioned whether that would apply to AI Overviews.

    Citation data you pull for AI Mode or AI Overviews this month now spans a model change on Nov. 12. The change applies to AI Mode’s default answers and to the hardest AI Overview questions.

    Nov. 12 falls inside the core update window, which began Nov. 10. Logging both dates lets you compare your tracking data before and after each one, rather than reading this month as a single change.

    Google’s claim that there are more links doesn’t include figures. You can check how it applies to your site by looking at the citation and referral numbers in your own reports.

    Although the Search Status Dashboard shows that the November core revision is rolling out, its completion date will be logged as the second date, after Nov. 12.

    You should watch for an announcement from Google on which AI Overview questions are classified as hardest so you can see how much of your AI Overview tracking will reflect the change.

    Diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

    According to recent reports, our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

    Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

    Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

    According to recent reports, xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

    The Chief Customer Officer is a fresh role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay. This is a customer-focused role in the most commercial sense: what a member earns from us, not the feature we shipped, is the centre of every decision.

    The measure of success is a Customer P&L that grows on what members hold and keep: LTV:CAC improving, approved-to-paid rising, churn falling, and customer contribution the business can strategy against.

    According to recent reports, this is a banking role, not a requirements-gathering role, a marketing role, or a role you can run from a dashboard. Products are priced on the balance sheet and judged on the money they attract and keep.

    Industry observers note that this part matters as much as the mandate. The known failure mode for this role, in any company, is a CCO with a polished customer-insight deck and no ownership of the number. That is disqualifying here.

    Day 30: The Customer P&L baseline is documented across retail and institutional: customer contribution, LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, net paid-member growth, and assets attracted and kept. You have formed your own independent view of where members are won, lost, and under-served, and shared it with the CEO and Board.Day 60: The unified Customer operating model is live: one set of key results across Growth, Client Coverage, Mission PMs, and Product Design, read weekly from one source. Every mission PM owns a product's contribution and its price, and the roadmap is ranked on what it earns, built with Finance and the line leads.Day 90: At least one measurable improvement in LTV:CAC, approved-to-paid, churn, or net upcoming AUM flow is live and attributable to a change you made, not a feature ship, an outcome moved. Every cell in your line has defined key results and an owner who explains the number every week.

    Impact Globally, Work Remotely.

    Shape the FutureImprove lives through cutting-edge technology, work 100% remotely from anywhere in the world.

    Industry observers note that great work-life balanceBuild amazing things with a balance of autonomy and collaborative teamwork. Set your own work schedule and make use of a flexible PTO blueprint when you need to recharge.

    Sources indicate that expect ExcellenceCollaborate, learn, and grow with a high-performance team. Learn how you learn best - from books to conferences, you’ll get a yearly budget for your individual learning and development goals.

    At Xapo, we prioritize consumer protection and adhere to regulatory requirements by ensuring that all Xapiens are accountable for upholding principles of fair treatment, transparency, and ethical conduct in their interactions with customers and stakeholders.
