    I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier mentioned than done.

    📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • It has been revealed that we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    It has been revealed that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    In a recent development, the claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

    Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

    Industry observers note that or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

    This wasn’t a totally latest experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

    It has been revealed that in this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

    I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

    Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

    Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

    According to recent reports, gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

    Me: So where did the number come from?

    Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

    Me: Does the book contain the original research?

    Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

    Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

    Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

    Sources indicate that lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research highlights that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

    In a recent development, I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

    Industry observers note that next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s manufacturer asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

    Sources indicate that I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research firm Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

    It has been revealed that there were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

    I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

    “I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

    Industry observers note that there is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she remarked. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

    According to recent reports, I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

    In a recent development, “It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”.

    Her conclusion: “It’s hard to source.”.

    The problem, Schneider mentioned, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody notes something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”.

    This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

    In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

    Sources indicate that it’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

    In a recent development, newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

    AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

    Sources indicate that “The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”.

    Sources indicate that most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

    When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than latest misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.).

    According to recent reports, nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

    Sources indicate that that’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

    Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

    Elizabeth Bromstein is a writer, editor, and perfumer.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Ads is rolling out a new Invalid Traffic Overview Card that shows advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.
    • Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information.
    • Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Ads is rolling out a new Invalid Traffic Overview Card that shows advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.

    Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information. The newly introduced card brings those figures into one view, with additional reporting available by day and campaign.

    Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.

    The global rollout began this week, and the feature is also available in Search Ads 360 for Google Ads accounts.

    Advertisers can find the new card on the Google Ads Overview page, under the Campaigns tab.

    Google has long used automated systems and manual reviews to filter invalid ad interactions, including bot activity, accidental clicks, and attempts to artificially inflate traffic.

    Most of that activity is caught before billing, so advertisers aren’t charged for those interactions.

    The new card includes three reporting areas:.

    Recent findings suggest that clicking “View details” opens a daily trend chart and campaign table. Advertisers can also access the monthly invoices where credits were applied.

    The estimated savings figure is the main addition to this information. Advertisers could already review invalid click metrics, but those reports didn’t show the estimated dollar amount Google had prevented from being charged.

    According to Marvin, Google’s systems catch the majority of invalid traffic before it reaches an advertiser’s invoice.

    Google Ads locks standard campaign metrics at month-end to match billing records. If Google detects more invalid traffic after that, any credits issued won’t change the Cost or CPA figures in the main Campaigns table.

    Advertisers who want to see those adjustments reflected in their performance metrics can use the Invalid Activity Credit: Search & PMax report.

    Available in Report editor, it includes 10 columns, such as Adjusted cost and Adjusted cost / conv. Credits are attributed to the dates the ads originally ran, even when Google issued them later.

    This gives advertisers a way to review Search and Performance Max costs with post-billing invalid activity credits factored in, without relying solely on the standard Campaigns table.

    The campaign-level breakdowns should make it easier to see where Google is filtering invalid activity, although the estimated savings figures will need some context.

    A campaign with significantly more spend could show higher estimated savings simply because it’s generating more traffic. Comparing those dollar amounts alone won’t necessarily tell advertisers which campaigns have greater traffic quality concerns.

    According to recent reports, there’s also a limit to what the numbers can tell us. The card reflects activity Google’s systems have identified as invalid, but it doesn’t establish how much fraudulent traffic may have gone undetected.

    For lead generation accounts, invalid traffic reporting won’t necessarily explain why fake or low-quality leads are continuing to come in.

    Marvin addressed this in the Ads Decoded newsletter: Google’s systems can filter invalid ad interactions, but bad leads can still come from legitimate clicks or submissions that never originated from an ad.

    Recent findings suggest that an account could have relatively little invalid traffic reported in Google Ads and still struggle with lead quality. Advertisers dealing with those issues will need to compare the reporting against their CRM data rather than assuming Google’s invalid traffic figures tell the whole story.

    What do we mean when we talk about news deserts?

    Recent findings suggest that the term has become a shorthand for areas devoid of local news coverage. But a new essay from the Independent Journalism Atlas recalls that when Penny Abernathy popularized the term through her research, she used it to describe a more nuanced picture:.

    Things grow in a desert, she told Medill’s Tim Franklin in 2024, just not as abundantly. Asked why she didn’t say “news vacuum,” she answered, “There’s news; it’s just not necessarily the quality and the quantity of what you would find elsewhere.” RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026To show what information can look like in news deserts, the Independent Journalism Atlas — an initiative that aims to “[document] independent creators who inform, educate, and advance public knowledge outside traditional media structures,” cofounded by Liz Kelly Nelson, Justin Bank, and 2025 Nieman Fellow Ryan Kellett — took a closer look at 46 of the 238 news desert counties identified in this year’s State of Local News report from Medill. RELATED ARTICLEMany people who live in “local news deserts” don’t feel deprived of local news, study findsLaura Hazard OwenFebruary 10, 2026“Look at the ground and news moves like water,” writes Bank. “It doesn’t stop at a county line. It runs off the surface, sinks underground and comes up wherever someone digs.” The team found that “in more places than the desert map shows, someone has picked up a shovel.” (That might help explain why people who live in news deserts don’t feel deprived of local news.) The team identifies a few patterns in how information looks and travels in news deserts, including “surface” information, wells, and springs. Posts from the local sheriff, weather alerts, and obituaries from the funeral home are all examples of “surface” information that “runs off,” Bank writes, typically telling you what happened without telling you why. Wells are newsrooms that form when a local paper shutters. The team points to the Anaconda Weekly Review in Deer Lodge County, Montana, as an example of a well appearing in a county Medill identified as a news desert. Springs, meanwhile, are “harder to spot” than wells because they’re smaller and more ad hoc. The Independent Journalism Atlas applies this label to efforts like the Gallatin County Board Illinois Unofficial Facebook page, which livestreams the board’s public meetings and posts its agendas. The team also paid attention to coverage of news deserts by outlets in neighboring counties. They found high school sports are often a gateway to coverage, pointing to a channel covering southern Illinois high school sports that interviewed the principal in Harrisburg, the seat of Saline County, another news desert county. RELATED ARTICLEUniversities are mapping where local news outlets are still thriving — and where gaps persistCorey HutchinsJanuary 16, 2025In recent years, efforts to “map” local news through different lenses have proliferated. The Independent Journalism Atlas is one such effort, focused on news creators. A better understanding of information sources in news deserts matters, Bank argues, because “you can’t tend a basin you haven’t mapped.” Read the full essay here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California is urging Meta not to implement its forthcoming commercial terms on November 20, his office confirmed Tuesday.

    In a letter sent to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Schiff called on the firm to respond by Monday, November 2 with the specific steps it will take to address user concerns.

    Sources indicate that “Forcing publishers to choose between surrendering their off-platform IP or forfeiting a primary channel of public communication is a gross abuse of Meta’s power as a powerful platform with critical access to consumers,” Schiff wrote. “Meta must not nullify federal IP protections and fair market competition through the unilateral insertion of fine print into terms of service contracts.”.

    Specifically, Schiff told Meta that it should “provide explicit guarantees that external technical boundaries like paywalls and robots.txt protocols will be fully respected.”.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEMeta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.Hanaa' TameezOctober 26, 2026“Meta’s verbal assurances that it will not supersede robots.txt files, which are voluntary server flags, do not appear to constitute enforceable legal protections,” Schiff wrote. “Without the insertion of specific language codifying Meta’s policy to respect robots.txt signals into the latest contractual terms, customers lack any reliable means by which to protect their content.”.

    Schiff’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    Schiff is the latest elected official in the United States to raise concerns about Meta’s commercial terms, which have now drawn bipartisan criticism. On Friday, Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee stated that the terms “indicate Meta is attempting to exploit American creators and businesses by granting itself sweeping authority to scrape content from any website associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts.”.

    Blackburn, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law, called on the company to withdraw the terms.

    It has been revealed that the terms were previously set to take effect on October 30. Because the terms offered no way to opt out, news of them set off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. Meta then delayed the effective date of its fresh terms of service for business accounts to November 20.

    On Tuesday, a coalition of Norwegian news publishers sued Meta over the terms and is asking the Oslo District Court to block the terms from going into effect. The legal action, led by the Norwegian Media Companies Association, is the first known lawsuit filed against Meta over its commercial terms.

    “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

    In a recent development, A Meta spokesperson mentioned on October 17 that the tech giant revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”.

    Sources indicate that as of October 27, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No version of the terms includes language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    #20519. What Reddit Reviews Reveals About Your Products via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (792 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    What Reddit Reviews Reveals About Your Products via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if Reddit’s taught us anything over the last five years, it’s that people really do care about validating the assumptions that they’re making along their journey.
    • Sources indicate that people want to see the questions, complaints, and comparisons that come up when they are deciding what to buy.
    • 10, Reddit announced the Reviews test with summaries of product conversations, themes about what people like and dislike, commonly compared products, and comments that lead back to their original discussions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if Reddit’s taught us anything over the last five years, it’s that people really do care about validating the assumptions that they’re making along their journey. They really want to hear from real consumers who have actually used something or tried something, what their experience was, even if they don’t know who those users are.

    Sources indicate that people want to see the questions, complaints, and comparisons that come up when they are deciding what to buy. Reddit Reviews brings those conversations together on one page, giving people another way to find those experiences and click through to the original discussions.

    On Nov. 10, Reddit announced the Reviews test with summaries of product conversations, themes about what people like and dislike, commonly compared products, and comments that lead back to their original discussions. Reddit states the initial rollout will reach U.S. owners in English on web, iOS, and Android. It covers about 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel. It prepares to add products and categories and expand beyond the U.S. during 2027.

    That can make research easier to inspect. A shopper can move from a summary to the comment, see the community where it appeared, and follow the details that matter to them. Reddit notes some pages will also include images, prices, and purchase links supplied through brand and retailer catalogs. Those details are worth checking, especially when a page’s price or product information does not match the retailer’s current listing.

    See also: Why Your Product Feed Is An SEO Asset (And Who Should Own It).

    According to recent reports, reddit Reviews can help surface patterns, but there are limitations explained in the page FAQs. A verified purchase is not required; Reddit does not confirm that someone bought or used a product, and AI can miss context. The sentiment display gives a quick view of included conversations, while the detailed comments show what went into it. A review cannot represent every customer or provide an exact percentage.

    According to recent reports, before drawing a conclusion from a review about your brand, I would ask: Is the same complaint coming up in different threads? Is the summary missing a condition that changes the recommendation? Are people comparing your product with a competitor for a reason your team has not been tracking? That context is where the useful research is.

    According to recent reports, A moderator’s concern was raised in the launch discussion about figuring out whether product recommendations come from people with firsthand experience. One commenter said verifying whether book recommendations came from people who had read the books was “already a gigantic challenge.” The moderator’s comment does not measure how Reddit Reviews performs, but it does point to a real trust question for any system summarizing community advice.

    See also: The Review Gap: Finding Client Opportunities In Competitor Feedback.

    I would treat these review pages as another place for brands to listen. Check whether a review exists for the products and categories you care about, compare its summary with the source comments, note the products people consider alongside yours, and check whether the merchant information is current. Then compare recurring questions and objections with what support, product, and research teams already hear.

    According to recent reports, that can tell you where expectations and experience diverge. It cannot tell you what all customers think, how many people bought, or whether Reviews changed a purchase. Reddit indicates the initial pages draw from eligible conversations and that businesses cannot pay for product inclusion.

    Sources indicate that there is no conversion result to claim yet. So, watch how review pages appear in Reddit search, and check the referral and conversion data available on your own site before drawing conclusions about sales.

    This is also a reason to make the community conversations themselves better. Give people room to ask real questions, share tradeoffs, and explain what did or did not work. If your team participates, be clear about who you are and help where you are welcome. My earlier piece on Reddit and the purchase journey makes the same point: People use Reddit to validate a decision, and the experience behind the recommendation is what gives that conversation value.

    This is why we work with all of our clients to make sure that we’re building a community for them where their users have a place to come and share and talk about their products and their experiences.

    Industry observers note that when you spot a recurring product problem or a comparison buyers keep making, take it back to the team that can do something with it. That is the kind of information I think marketers can actually use.

    Breaking: Creators who show their sources build trust, survey finds

    • Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Journalist-led research found audiences increased trust when news videos identified their sources, such as government documents and interviews.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLETwo-thirds of news influencers are men — and most have never worked for a news organizationSarah ScireNovember 18, 2024About one in five U.S. adults regularly gets their news from news creators on social media platforms, but it can be difficult for audiences to suss out which personalities to trust amid an avalanche of misinformation, hot takes, and polarizing content.

    New research spearheaded by a team of journalists and political scientists highlights that giving audiences a peek into the reporting process can help bolster their trust in the news.

    According to recent reports, proof News, a nonprofit newsroom focused on tech accountability, in collaboration with researchers at the French university Sciences Po, shared social news videos with 2,000 U.S. adults to measure their perceptions of trustworthiness. Participants were randomly assigned one of Proof’s yet-to-be-published short-form news videos.

    Some participants viewed videos with labels describing the sources, others saw videos with labels describing the newsroom’s ethical standards, and some saw videos without a label. The Sources labels appeared on cards embedded at the end of the video, like a credits reel, or were placed into the video description, the text accompanying the video.

    Participants then rated the videos on various trust metrics. We found that labeling videos did increase trust — particularly a label that described the video sources in the description and, to a slightly lesser extent, a label describing newsroom standards in the credits.

    It has been revealed that this effect was particularly prominent among survey respondents who identified as Democrats or reported having high trust in science. Those groups, when shown the sourcing label in the description of a general news video, reported higher assessments of transparency and trust in the journalist.

    There were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with labels for text articles, but Sally Lehrman, founder of The Trust Project, remarked the findings were still intriguing.

    It has been revealed that “I’m excited to see the results,” Lehrman noted. “Methods and references really do resonate…People are asking, where did the journalist get this information, and how can I trust it.”.

    As audiences increasingly turn to social media for news, there is a growing public discussion about how trustworthy creators are, especially when it comes to disclosing their funding and relationships. In January, The Wall Street Journal wrote about corporate and foreign interests using influencers to push agendas. In August, The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon secretly hired conservative military veterans with large online audiences to amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s messaging, and a Upcoming York Times investigation revealed online influencers received funding from political campaigns without disclosing the connection in their videos.

    Some creators have begun trying to distinguish themselves from this type of behavior through their own disclosure efforts.

    RELATED ARTICLEWith Local News International, Dave Jorgenson becomes his own TikTok guyNeel DhaneshaSeptember 9, 2025Journalist and creator Dave Jorgenson, who has nearly 1 million followers across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, has started publishing a transparency report on his website, Local News International, revealing his sources of funding alongside his editorial standards.

    Ultimately, he thinks disclosures of political funding should no longer be voluntary but mandatory. “Platforms should be regulating themselves,” Jorgenson said in an interview. “You can’t really force that unless there are laws.”.

    Proof used Jorgenson’s ethics and transparency statement as a model for the newsroom standards label in video testing and found that it increased viewers’ trust in the news outlet and the likelihood that they would share a general news story.

    Recent findings suggest that upcoming York City is already considering disclosure requirements in the wake of revelations in the Columbia Journalism Review that exposed the inner workings of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s connections with influencers. The author of the article, Anya Schiffrin, a senior lecturer at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, testified at a September city council meeting that creator relationships — both paid and unpaid — should be disclosed to viewers.

    “It’s key for democracy that we have standards,” Schiffrin remarked.

    RELATED ARTICLEProof News is Julia Angwin’s attempt to bring the scientific method to investigative journalismNeel DhaneshaMarch 21, 2024Proof News, which launched in 2024, pioneered an Ingredients label that takes cues from the scientific method and names the journalists’ hypothesis, sources, limitations, and the story’s findings.

    To test whether the label worked to increase viewer trust for short-form vertical videos, we stripped down the Ingredients label to a bullet list of sources followed by an asterisk denoting the reporting limitations. The survey highlighted the label had a consistent positive effect when placed in the video description, the text box that is often located under the video.

    According to recent reports, the team also tested how labels performed on online text news articles. The survey demonstrated 1,600 U.S. participants original, unpublished Proof News stories without a label, with a Proof Ingredients label, a label modeled after the Trust Project that described the reporting process, and a label describing newsroom standards.

    In a recent development, there were fewer statistically significant increases in trust metrics with the print labels. The most significant findings were an increase in perception of transparency when the reporting process label was used on a polarizing story and an investigative story.

    One possible explanation for the differing results between labeling video and text articles is the “ergonomics” of the medium, said Damien Bol, a professor at the Center for Political Research at Sciences Po who helped lead the survey design and data analysis.

    According to recent reports, “When reading a text, for example, people can quickly skim through it or skip parts of it, whereas a video forces them to follow the story second by second, even when watching at double speed,” Bol noted. Different formats, Bol said, shape the “experience of consuming a news story.”.

    Earlier this month, Julia Angwin, an author of this article, hosted a private convening of creators at Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy to discuss creating shared standards that could be conveyed through a label or other public statement.

    The group of 30 leading content creators from news, science communication, education, history, and other evidence-based fields discussed how they could distinguish their work by signaling to viewers their commitment to standards that could include disclosing funding sources and the use of artificial intelligence. Creator-led efforts to bring this to fruition are ongoing.

    San Diego-based journalist Lisa Remillard, who has more than 4 million followers on her TikTok channel “The News Girl,” remarked that making videos with verified facts can feel like a small club. But if she can’t independently confirm something, she’s “not putting that out there.”.

    It has been revealed that remillard’s audience appears to appreciate transparency. Earlier this year, she published a video describing her editorial standards — and was richly rewarded for it. “I think clearly defining those ethics and standards resonated with my audience and gave them a reason to want to financially support my work,” Remillard remarked.

    Jessica Yellin, the founder of the political podcast, YouTube channel, and social media brand “News Not Noise,” has also called for news creators to voluntarily sign a Creator Constitution, agreeing to journalistic standards such as citing sources, fixing errors, and disclosing financial relationships.

    She remarked labeling sources is about the “signal.” Even if audiences don’t take the time to digest every word, Yellin observed, “It’s the act of showing it that matters.”.

    According to recent reports, julia Angwin is the founder of Proof News and the founding director of the Independent Media + Audience Project at the Shorenstein Center on Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. Annie Gilbertson is managing editor of Proof News. Rina Palta is editor-at-large at Proof News and senior data scientist at the Independent Media + Audience Project.

    #20514. 72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1977 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    72% Of Worker’s Say Their AI Skills Are Untested – Here’s How PPC Managers Prove Theirs via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are.
    • Fresh research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S.
    • I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you manage Google Ads accounts, being “good” with AI is expected, but employers probably never checked (or didn’t know how to check) if you are. Being able to show your judgment is a career must if you can, and a risk if you can’t.

    Fresh research from CodeSignal surveyed 1,000 U.S. employees and 1,000 U.S. people managers about AI readiness, and two numbers sit side by side in the results. 72% of workers surveyed say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, yet 69% of managers call AI ability a major or moderate factor in hiring. Indicating that employers are hiring for a skill they mostly don’t measure.

    I sent CodeSignal 15 questions about how solid those numbers are and what practitioners should do about them. The written answers were more candid than I expected, including on the obvious conflict of interest of an assessment vendor concluding that nobody assesses anything. Here’s what holds up, what needs a footnote, and what it means for people who run paid search for a living.

    Industry observers note that start with what this survey is and isn’t. CodeSignal commissioned two online surveys through Pollfish in September 2026, and both samples were entirely U.S.-based. The firm defined knowledge workers by the work they do rather than by job title, meaning people whose jobs run mainly on computers and digital tools. It also didn’t screen out people who skip AI. 12% mentioned they never use it at work.

    In a recent development, codeSignal reports that roles where AI use is required or expected “jumped 78%.” I asked whether that meant percentage points. It doesn’t. It’s a relative increase, self-reported by employees about their own roles, measured across each person’s time in their current job. When respondents started those jobs, 9.4% remarked AI use was required or expected of them. Today, 16.7% say so.

    According to recent reports, that’s nearly double. It’s also fewer than one in five.

    Paid search people are probably well past that curve already, since automated bidding has been Google’s default recommendation for years. So, the useful question for our field is whether anyone can tell who is using AI well.

    See also: From T-Shaped To M-Shaped: The PPC Career Evolution Nobody Is Talking About.

    It has been revealed that 62% of employees told CodeSignal they received employer training on how to use AI at work. Only 35% said employer training is where they built the AI skills they actually use.

    Industry observers note that I asked whether most of that training simply wasn’t about AI, or whether workers weren’t counting it. CodeSignal noted neither. The training was specifically about using AI at work, and the firm reads the gap as a sign that it wasn’t substantial or specific enough to apply on the job.

    The follow-up number is worse. Only about one in four trained workers said they can apply most or all of their employer’s AI training. The other 74% apply some, very little, or none of it. Run that against the full sample and roughly 46% of all workers got AI training they can’t fully use. When CodeSignal asked what gets in the way, employees named lack of time, training that doesn’t fit their role, and lack of access to relevant training.

    So, where are people learning? The question allowed multiple answers, which is why the figures don’t add up to 100. Free resources people found on their own led at 46%, followed by trial and error on the job at 39%, and employer training at 35%. Colleagues came in at 22%, and courses people paid for themselves at 12%.

    Tigran Sloyan, CodeSignal’s co-founder and CEO, noted, “Companies are buying AI courses or building their own, but if most workers are going elsewhere to learn, you have to wonder if that training is actually helping.”.

    Paid search has worked this way for a long time. Plenty of PPC managers learned bidding by watching their own accounts and reading practitioners on LinkedIn and X. What has changed is that the thing they now learn by trial and error is the ad platform’s own AI, and each error is paid for out of a client’s budget.

    According to recent reports, 72% of workers say their AI skills have never been formally evaluated, but 66% say the same about their skills in general. That’s a six-point gap.

    It has been revealed that I asked CodeSignal whether the real story is that companies don’t assess much of anything, and AI just makes that visible. The answer began with “Yes, exactly.” Companies have long made people decisions on proxies such as resumes, job titles, tenure, and manager impressions. CodeSignal’s argument is that those were always weak signals, and they get costly when roles shift in months. More than six in ten managers in the survey said they make people decisions based on assumptions rather than reliable data.

    This bothers me more in paid media than almost anywhere else. We measure campaigns to the decimal point. We argue about attribution windows, incrementality tests, and conversion lag. Then we judge the people running those campaigns with a once-a-year “meets expectations.” For a discipline built on measurement, that’s a strange double standard, and AI is making it harder to defend.

    Recent findings suggest that codeSignal says the hiring side already indicates the strain. When AI fluency is a criterion nobody has measured, people get judged on what’s easy to see, such as who is most visible or sounds most confident, instead of on the quality of their work.

    It has been revealed that anyone who has sat through an agency pitch knows how that plays out. The person who says the automation will figure it out can sound more fluent than the person who spent the afternoon reading search terms and adding negatives. Only one of them is protecting the budget.

    It has been revealed that “A resume is a story someone tells about their skills,” Sloyan remarked. “The work is the proof. Right now, most companies are making their biggest decisions about people based on the story.”.

    See also: PPC Automation Layering: How Smart Advertisers Combine Automation With Strategy.

    Sources indicate that I asked CodeSignal to separate “AI fluency” from AI literacy and prompt-writing, because those terms get used as if they were the same thing. The organization drew the lines this way. Literacy means understanding what AI is. Prompt-writing is a tactic. Fluency means knowing what to delegate to AI, checking and correcting its output, and recognizing when not to use it at all.

    That is the best short job description for a modern PPC manager I’ve read this year.

    Map it onto a Google Ads account, and each part becomes something you can point to. Delegation is deciding which campaigns get Smart Bidding, which conversion actions you feed it, and what budget it gets to learn on. Checking is reading the search terms, placements, and automatically created assets that the system produces, then correcting what’s wrong. Knowing when not to use AI is the judgment call that rarely demonstrates up in a dashboard. That might mean holding back a campaign with too little conversion data, or keeping a human hand on ad copy in a regulated category.

    Industry observers note that none of that is visible in a certificate. All of it is visible in the account.

    See also: The Conversion Setup Errors That Break Smart Bidding.

    I also asked CodeSignal to critique its own product category. What can a timed, simulated assessment not tell you about whether someone uses AI well on the job? The company answered that an assessment is only as useful as what it was designed and validated to measure. To understand how someone performs over time, it stated, you need to look at their actual work.

    Sources indicate that that answer applies just as well to the credential most PPC people already hold. Google’s AI-Powered Performance Ads Certification on Skillshop is free, and third-party study guides describe it as a timed, 50-question exam. It’s worth taking, because it teaches how Google wants its AI campaign types used. But it’s written by the platform whose recommendations a good PPC manager sometimes overrides. Passing it shows you know Google’s playbook. It can’t show the afternoon you decided not to follow it, or what happened to cost per acquisition when you didn’t.

    Industry observers note that then there’s the conflict of interest. CodeSignal sells assessments, and its survey concludes that skills aren’t being assessed. I asked how readers should weigh that, and what finding cut against its business.

    In a recent development, the organization remarked its interest in skills is the reason it commissioned the study. Then it volunteered a number that does cut the other way. 82% of employees said their manager understands their skills very or somewhat well. CodeSignal called that knowledge real and valuable. Its caveat is that the knowledge is informal, varies from manager to manager, doesn’t follow people when they change teams, and can’t be compared across a company.

    Sources indicate that agency people will recognize that last part. When an account manager moves to another client team, everything their old boss knew about their judgment usually stays behind.

    Industry observers note that I give CodeSignal credit for offering up the 82%. I’d still want to see the full questionnaire before treating any of these figures as settled, and the organization’s launch announcement for its Agentic Skills Intelligence product doesn’t describe the survey method at all. The details above came from its answers to my questions.

    CodeSignal’s advice to individual workers was blunt. Saying you use AI for everything doesn’t prove much. Fluency is being able to explain exactly how you use it and, just as important, when you don’t. For a PPC manager, that turns into a short routine.

    If you lead a PPC team or run an agency, the manufacturer’s advice for a 200-person business with no assessment budget translates well. Start with managers, since most employees think their managers already understand their skills. Then give those managers something more concrete than “meets expectations” by writing down what good AI use looks like for each role on the team. A specialist’s standard might be catching irrelevant search terms within a week. A strategist’s might be deciding when a client’s conversion tracking is clean enough to move to value-based bidding.

    Industry observers note that next, look at real account work before training and again after it. A sample of a few accounts per person is enough to see whether anything changed.

    According to recent reports, find your self-taught experts, too. With 46% of workers learning from free resources on their own, someone on your team has probably already worked out what the automation gets wrong. Have them show everyone else.

    According to recent reports, finally, build training around the work people do every week and give them time to practice. Lack of time was the obstacle employees named first. Track whether people use what they learned, not whether they finished the course. A Skillshop badge is a completion metric, and you’d never let a client judge a campaign on impressions alone.

    Sloyan’s version of this is worth quoting. “Training only works when it’s built around the job someone actually does.”.

    Recent findings suggest that my view is that PPC managers have an advantage most knowledge workers in this survey don’t. Our work already leaves a record. Every bid strategy change, every negative keyword, and every recommendation we dismissed is logged somewhere, with performance data attached.

    According to recent reports, most of us treat that record as housekeeping. The managers who turn it into evidence of judgment are the ones who will get promoted while their employers are still figuring out how to measure AI skills at all.

    Everyone else will be telling a story.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Vox owners can watch videos and listen to podcasts in the app, but reading stories requires a paid subscription.

    Vox has debuted its first mobile application, the publication best known for its explanatory journalism announced Wednesday morning.

    In a recent development, growing membership is a “key priority,” managing editor for audience and membership Bill Carey remarked. Vox believes launching the app is one way to do that. A Vox membership costs $5 per month, or $60 per year, and offers ad-free versions of podcasts and unlimited access to all of the website’s contents.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLEVox is revamping its editorial strategy to redefine what ‘Voxxy’ meansHanaa' TameezNovember 8, 2021Strengthening its relationship to its audience is only becoming more important for Vox. The app launch comes at a time when news publishers are increasingly trying to keep consumers on their own platforms amid growing preferences for AI summaries, news creators, and industry-wide traffic declines.

    In a recent development, “The move toward developing our membership program in the last couple of years has really been about understanding how key it is for us to build more community and to foster that loyalty [of our] audience,” Carey said. “When we were looking at that, it really felt like an app was a good way to continue pointing in that direction.”.

    Vox isn’t the only news outlet focusing on mobile apps. The Verge — Vox’s former sister publication under Vox Media — named traffic declines as one of the reasons why it prepares to launch its own app next year. The Wall Street Journal’s head of digital, Taneth Evans, recently noted that the Journal makes its app more useful to users by offering all of its mediums in one place. Evans also said that news publishers “need to give people reasons to open an app beyond simply offering news.”.

    “Websites will become a service for agents,” Evans mentioned. “Apps are gonna be the thing that humans will connect with.”.

    Vox declined to provide website traffic numbers, but data from Comscore shows that the website’s unique visitors decreased by 36% year-over-year between September 2025 (7.4 million) and September 2026 (4.8 million). Archived data from SimilarWeb shows the site had 20.8 million visits in September 2021.

    Sources indicate that “Vox isn’t immune to the larger trends that have led to web traffic declines in recent years, but those only represent a portion of our audience,” Carey said in an email. “Vox is focused on building audience engagement across platforms, with social video views up 86% year-over-year and newsletter audience up 14%.”.

    Sources indicate that “Even if there wasn’t a decline in search traffic, as everyone has been seeing — and we still get members from search — we want to create that relationship with our audience,” publisher and editor-in-chief Swati Sharma said. “People know Vox and they have a relationship with Vox. We have a younger audience that’s on all of these different platforms. I think it is definitely a part of building that relationship ourselves.”.

    That the app makes all Vox content accessible in one place for current and future members also signals the “un-siloing” of the newsroom overall, Sharma noted. Vox currently has 78 editorial employees.

    Industry observers note that RELATED ARTICLESwati Sharma is leading a new era in Vox’s mission to “explain the world”Hanaa' TameezMay 6, 2021When Sharma, who has helmed Vox.com since 2021, first arrived, she found that Vox’s main mediums (text, audio, and video) “weren’t in service of one another.” The “silos” allowed teams to build their own audiences and products. But while teams discussed story ideas with each other and during editorial meetings, “they all [needed] to go into their creative spaces and find what works for their medium and not be in service of just one larger section.”.

    According to recent reports, that’s changed over the past five years, Sharma noted. Each team — text, video, and audio — does a little bit of everything now. Text reporters appear on podcasts and in videos, while podcasters and hosts also write their own newsletters.

    It has been revealed that “In a lot of newsrooms, there’s one dominant form, and at Vox, there wasn’t. They’re all really notable,” Sharma said. “[Senior correspondent] Dylan Scott is on our Unexplainable podcast talking about Alzheimer’s. [Host and editorial director] Astead Herndon does a newsletter and a Substack Live every week, and he does a podcast. That’s the future for us, and that’s where our whole newsroom is moving, where those silos are done and you can basically do everything.”.

    Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Meta will complete “a full consultation” with news industry leaders before implementing its controversial new terms — even if it means another delay, an executive for the social media company revealed today.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms upgrade. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms. Until then our existing terms remain in place.”.

    Meta did not answer Nieman Lab’s questions about which news industry groups and leaders Meta aims to consult.

    Industry observers note that the proposed terms have drawn criticism because they would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and potentially allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models, with no option to opt out. Last week, Meta announced it would push back implementation of its new terms to November 20 in order to “explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab. Meta had previously revised its new terms to remove the word “train.” No version of the terms has included language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

    Shortly after Stone’s announcement, a Norwegian court blocked Meta’s terms from taking effect on November 20 until the court had assessed their legality, the country’s public broadcaster NRK reported.

    In a recent development, “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the latest terms are unreasonable,” mentioned Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL’s board chair, in a news release. “We are also pleased that the court recognizes that the alternative is that media companies risk losing control over editorial content built up over many years.”.

    Since Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15, publishers and politicians around the world have pushed back, filing complaints with national competition authorities, calling on the European Commission to investigate, and writing letters to Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Two United States senators — California Democrat Adam Schiff and Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn — each separately wrote to Zuckerberg, insisting that the company withdraw the terms as they’re right now written.

    “After I raised serious concerns about Meta’s prepares to scrape and abuse creators’ content, I am pleased the tech giant is finally acknowledging the concerns of publishers and content creators,” Blackburn stated in a statement to Nieman Lab on Wednesday. “While this is a step in the right direction, a vague promise to consult with industry stakeholders and potentially delay implementation is not nearly enough. Meta must commit to meaningful changes that protect the intellectual property rights of American creators, and I will continue holding the company accountable until it does.”.

    On October 21, the European Publishers Council signed onto a joint letter to the European Commission, asking the Commission to block the terms from taking effect. The letter claims that Meta’s terms violate the Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of major tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

    EPC executive director Angela Mills Wade said on Wednesday that the organization has not heard from Meta about its letter or its concerns.

    Recent findings suggest that “We welcome Meta’s offer to consult publishers fully, and to delay implementation if necessary,” Mills Wade remarked in an email to Nieman Lab. “However, that consultation must lead to binding contractual safeguards…Using Meta’s services to reach audiences or advertise should not mean granting wider rights to exploit publishers’ journalism, whether collected from websites or uploaded to its platforms. Publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.”.

    This story has been updated to include a statement from Marsha Blackburn.

    #20508. Industry News: Google Lets Target Frequency Pair Non-Skippable Ads With Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (820 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Google Lets Target Frequency Pair Non-Skippable Ads With Shorts via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google has revised its help page on Target frequency campaigns, which claims advertisers may now use non-skippable in-stream ads with Shorts and in-feed ads within the same campaign.
    • On this page, advertisers are allowed to “mix any combination of skippable in-stream, non-skippable in-stream (up to 20s), bumper, In-feed, and Shorts ads” in a campaign.
    • In a recent development, there is no date referenced on the page.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google has revised its help page on Target frequency campaigns, which claims advertisers may now use non-skippable in-stream ads with Shorts and in-feed ads within the same campaign.

    On this page, advertisers are allowed to “mix any combination of skippable in-stream, non-skippable in-stream (up to 20s), bumper, In-feed, and Shorts ads” in a campaign.

    In a recent development, there is no date referenced on the page. However, the capture by the Internet Archive from Oct. 14 still demonstrates the earlier rule: “Right now, non-skippable ads can’t be combined with In-feed or Shorts ads in Target Frequency campaigns.” Prior to the update, advertisers who were using the Target frequency option had to choose whether to use non-skippable ads or the Shorts and in-feed ad placements options.

    Campaigns limited to in-stream formats can’t add in-feed or Shorts, which Google’s page warns “may result in less reach or a higher cost-per-thousand impressions (CPM)” for those campaigns.

    Industry observers note that in the Oct. 14 version of the Target frequency page, selecting non-skippable ads would “automatically disable In-feed and Shorts ads” in the campaign. The current setup steps say to select the Non-skippable in-stream checkbox to include those ads “alongside your selected formats” in a multi-format campaign.

    It has been revealed that the page’s “up to 20s” label for non-skippable ads wasn’t in the Oct. 14 version. On Google’s Video reach campaigns page, the recommended non-skippable length for Target frequency went from 7 to 15 seconds in the Oct. 14 capture to 7 to 20 seconds now. That page’s Target frequency table now also lists in-feed and Shorts, and recommends a vertical video of 6 to 60 seconds next to horizontal 15- and 6-second videos.

    The current page lists a single frequency range of 2 to 7 per week or 4 to 12 per month. The Oct. 14 capture gave that range for multi-format campaigns and 2 to 4 per week (4 to 8 per month) for in-stream-only campaigns. When I covered Target frequency’s global launch in 2022, Google mentioned advertisers could pick a goal of up to four per week.

    The same Target frequency campaign may use both non-skippable video ads and either Shorts ads or in-feed ads; however, it will need to be limited to auction buying, as the help page makes reserve buying available on “non-mixed formats” only.

    While legacy campaigns which are in-stream-only cannot change from one ad format type to another once they are created (a rule also on the page before the patch), multi-format campaigns do allow changing the ad format types in campaign settings. At present (Nov. 12), the page does not provide information about what happens when adding non-skippable ads to a multi-format campaign created before the update to see if you can still include in-feed and Shorts ads without dropping them.

    The Target frequency campaign help page FAQ also explains that an existing campaign cannot be converted into a Target frequency campaign and instructs the advertiser to “end your current campaign and set up a latest Target frequency campaign” in its place.

    Recent findings suggest that at the time I looked at the English Target frequency page on Nov. 12, it demonstrated the new mixing rule. However, both the UK English and Australian English versions of the Target frequency page were stating you cannot mix in-feed or Shorts ad placements and non-skippable video ad placements. The UK English version of the setup guide continues to list a separate weekly range of 2 to 4 for in-stream formats.

    In addition, Display & Video 360’s own Target frequency help page which provides assistance for those purchasing using this channel reveals that non-skippable video ads are available “up to 15 seconds” only when purchased as an in-stream-only format.

    Google Ads Help’s Newly introduced features & announcements section had no announcement regarding the revision as of Nov. 12. The last announcement published there was dated May 20.

    Per Google’s updated help page, brands buying Target frequency at auction no longer have to choose between non-skippable ads and Shorts or in-feed reach.

    Prior to developing a campaign for Target frequency using auctions, you should create a fresh Target frequency campaign, open the Ad formats drop-down within that campaign and verify if selecting Non-skippable in-stream leaves both in-feed and Shorts selected within your account.

    The Video reach page says that horizontal video can serve on Shorts (when there is no vertical video in the ad group) and eligible horizontal videos may be served vertically when video enhancements are turned on.

    Google suggests creating vertical video content for Shorts and horizontal video content for feed ads and non-skippable ads.

    Watch for the UK and Australian versions of the Target frequency page to match the English page, and for any change to Display & Video 360’s page. Also watch the English page for a note on adding non-skippable ads to campaigns created before the enhancement.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    It has been revealed that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sometimes, adding just one fresh ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.11Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app.

    Here’s Genevieve Ko, NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, explaining the upcoming features:.

    I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.

    According to recent reports, the Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

    Say you’re cooking braised white beans and greens with parmesan, NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone22There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the latest AI feature could account for.

    Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”.

    In a recent development, but because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

    Broadly speaking, commenters weren’t buying it.

    According to recent reports, “What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”.

    Industry observers note that “This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” claims Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”.

    Industry observers note that “Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”.

    “PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” notes Judah Mann of Fresh York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”.

    Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”.

    Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the latest AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

    Sources indicate that dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

    Industry observers note that one consistent thread was that cooking is supposed to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”.

    Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the fresh AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” notes Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”.

    About six in 10 Americans noted they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a latest national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    The survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that showed trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    Industry observers note that the Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents remarked journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For years, bot management in SEO was relatively straightforward.
    • AI search has made that approach increasingly inadequate.
    • Sources indicate that today, websites are accessed by traditional search crawlers, AI training crawlers, retrieval bots, user-initiated fetches, and autonomous agents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For years, bot management in SEO was relatively straightforward. You either allowed crawlers to access your website or blocked them. That model was never perfect, but it was generally sufficient for what we needed.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    AI search has made that approach increasingly inadequate.

    Sources indicate that today, websites are accessed by traditional search crawlers, AI training crawlers, retrieval bots, user-initiated fetches, and autonomous agents. These serve very different purposes, yet we regularly lump them together under the term “AI bots.”.

    Blocking a crawler used for model training has different consequences from blocking one retrieving content for search answers – this distinction really matters!

    Robots.txt remains useful, but as it’s voluntary actual enforcement happens through CDNs, web application firewalls and bot mitigation services, which can contradict your robots.txt rules without the SEO team even knowing.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    Agents complicate matters further. They can browse websites like real owners, trigger analytics tracking, and become increasingly difficult to distinguish from human visitors. Block an agent performing a product comparison, and you might not simply lose a ranking. You could disappear from the answer entirely.

    It has been revealed that my argument is that we need to move from block lists to deliberate bot policies. Policies that consider who’s accessing our content, why they’re doing it and the consequences of allowing or blocking them.

    According to recent reports, these decisions increasingly involve SEO, engineering, security, legal, and commercial teams. They need to be coordinated, consistently enforced and regularly reviewed.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    In a recent development, I’ve covered these challenges, their implications, and some practical approaches in my GEO Elite presentation. Hope you find it useful:.

    This post was originally published on AI Search Marketing with Chris Green.
